Efficient Online Submodular Maximization with Bandit Feedback

Iasonas Nikolaou Affiliation: Boston University Email: nikolaou@bu.edu    Evimaria Terzi Affiliation: Boston University Email: evimaria@bu.edu
Abstract

We study online monotone submodular maximization under a cardinality constraint with bandit feedback. On each round, the learner selects at most kk elements from a ground set of size nn and observes only the value of the selected set. We develop an efficient algorithm achieving 𝒪⁡(k​n​T​log⁡(n/k))\mathcal{O}\!\left(k\sqrt{nT\log(n/k)}\right) expected (1−1/e)(1-1/e)-regret over TT rounds. To our knowledge, this is the first polynomial-time algorithm with T\sqrt{T} dependence on the horizon for arbitrary monotone submodular functions in the bandit setting. Our approach uses randomized sampling and a carefully constructed potential to reduce online submodular maximization to online linear optimization over the probability simplex.

1 Introduction

Submodular optimization is a central theme in machine learning. The key reason for that is that submodularity captures diminishing returns and arises in numerous applications including sensor placement (Krause and Guestrin, 2007), team formation (Bhowmik et al., 2014), caching networks (Li et al., 2021), influence maximization (Kempe et al., 2003), recommender systems (Nikolaou et al., 2025), and multi-robot planning (Xu et al., 2023). Motivated by these applications, a growing literature studies Online Submodular Maximization (OSM) under various settings (Streeter et al., 2009; Zhang et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2022; Si Salem et al., 2024).

In OSM, a learner, at each round tt, selects a set St⊆VS_{t}\subseteq V with |St|≤k|S_{t}|\leq k and observes a monotone submodular reward ftf_{t}. The goal is to minimize the expected (1−1/e)(1-1/e)-regret, i.e.,

ℛT1−1/e≔(1−1e)​max⁡∑t=1TS⊆V|S|≤k⁡ft​(S)−𝔼⁡[∑t=1Tft​(St)].\Reg_{T}^{1-1/e}\coloneqq\left(1-\frac{1}{e}\right)\max_{\begin{subarray}{c}S\subseteq V\\ |S|\leq k\end{subarray}}\sum_{t=1}^{T}f_{t}(S)-\mathbb{E}\!\left[\sum_{t=1}^{T}f_{t}(S_{t})\right].

This quantity compares the learner’s cumulative reward with that of the best fixed set in hindsight. The (1−1/e)(1-1/e) factor is necessary for polynomial-time algorithms due to the hardness results associated with the offline problem (Feige, 1998).

In this paper, we focus on Bandit-OSM, where at every round tt the learner only observes the value of the function on the selected set, i.e., ft​(St)f_{t}(S_{t}) (as opposed to receiving the whole ftf_{t}). The best existing results for Bandit-OSM achieve ℛT1−1/e=𝒪~​(T2/3)\Reg_{T}^{1-1/e}=\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(T^{2/3}) both for cardinality (Wan et al., 2023) and for general matroid constraints (Wan and Zhang, 2026).

This raises the question:

Is it possible to obtain a computationally efficient algorithm for Bandit-OSM with 𝒪⁡(T)\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{T}) expected (1−1/e)(1-1/e)-regret?

We answer this question affirmatively: to our knowledge, we develop the first polynomial-time algorithm that achieves 𝒪⁡(T)\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{T}) expected (1−1/e)(1-1/e)-regret for Bandit-OSM under cardinality constraints with arbitrary monotone submodular reward functions.

Our algorithm, Submodular-Exponential-Weights (Sub-EW), is a bandit exponential-weights method based on EXP3 (Auer et al., 2002). Sub-EW is conceptually simple: it maintains a distribution over the elements of VV. At each iteration, it randomly chooses how many elements to sample, draws them independently, and plays their union. Randomizing the number of draws makes it possible to estimate, from the observed reward, the gradient of a carefully-constructed potential. The resulting gradient estimate guides the exponential-weights update of the distribution over VV.

2 Related work

In this section, we give an overview of the existing results on Online Submodular Maximization (OSM) in the bandit setting (i.e., Bandit-OSM).

Bandit-OSM is considerably more challenging than its full-information counterpart: the learner observes only the value of the selected set and cannot directly evaluate marginal gains. Early work by Streeter and Golovin (2008) introduced the meta-action approach for online monotone submodular maximization under a cardinality constraint. Their bandit construction simulates the steps of the offline greedy algorithm using separate online learners and achieves ℛT1−1/e=𝒪~​(T2/3)\Reg_{T}^{1-1/e}=\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(T^{2/3}). Streeter et al. (2009) extended this approach to online assignment problems, a special case of partition matroid constraints, obtaining regret ℛT1−1/e\Reg_{T}^{1-1/e} of order 𝒪~​(T4/5)\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(T^{4/5}).

Niazadeh et al. (2023) developed a general offline-to-online reduction based on Blackwell approachability. Their framework transforms robust greedy approximation algorithms into online algorithms, yielding the bound ℛT1−1/e=𝒪⁡(T2/3)\Reg_{T}^{1-1/e}=\mathcal{O}(T^{2/3}) for Bandit-OSM. In a different direction, Zhang et al. (2019) introduced Bandit–Frank–Wolfe for online continuous DR-submodular maximization under bandit feedback, attaining ℛT1−1/e=𝒪⁡(T8/9)\Reg_{T}^{1-1/e}=\mathcal{O}(T^{8/9}). Their discrete counterpart, Responsive–Frank–Wolfe, uses responsive-bandit feedback, requiring evaluations at infeasible sets that yield zero reward.

Wan et al. (2023) reduced Bandit-OSM to bandit multilinear DR-submodular maximization, achieving ℛT1−1/e=𝒪~​(T2/3)\Reg_{T}^{1-1/e}=\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(T^{2/3}) under partition matroid constraints. More recently, Wan and Zhang (2026) obtained the expected regret bound ℛT1−1/e=𝒪~​(T2/3)\Reg_{T}^{1-1/e}=\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(T^{2/3}) for Bandit-OSM under general matroid constraints.

As summarized in Table 1, none of the above works achieves the regret bound ℛT1−1/e=𝒪⁡(T)\Reg_{T}^{1-1/e}=\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{T}) under cardinality constraints for Bandit-OSM, which is what we establish here.

To the best of our knowledge, the only other polynomial-time result achieving ℛT1−1/e=𝒪~​(T)\Reg_{T}^{1-1/e}=\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\sqrt{T}) under bandit feedback and cardinality constraints is due to Pasteris et al. (2024). Their analysis applies to monotone and submodular objectives that additionally satisfy pseudo-concavity, including sum-max functions. This class captures facility-location and kk-median rewards, coverage and hitting-set objectives, and best-of-kk bandits, but is a proper subclass of monotone submodular functions. In contrast, our guarantee holds for arbitrary monotone submodular rewards. At each round, their algorithm samples kk elements with replacement and plays their union. The observed reward is used to construct a gradient estimate for an exponential-weights update. The pseudo-concavity property yields a concave expected-reward potential. In contrast, we construct a weighted potential that combines expected rewards from different numbers of independent draws with replacement, ranging from one to kk. This potential allows us to handle arbitrary monotone submodular functions without assuming pseudo-concavity. By randomizing the number of draws, we obtain an unbiased estimate of the potential’s gradient from a single observed reward while retaining the (1−1/e)(1-1/e) approximation factor.

Stochastic submodular bandits.

A related literature considers a variant of our setting where the learner receives bandit feedback, but the reward functions are chosen stochastically (i.e., not adversarially). Nie et al. (2022) proposed an explore-then-commit greedy algorithm for this setting and stochastic monotone submodular rewards and cardinality constraints and established ℛT1−1/e=𝒪~​(T2/3)\Reg_{T}^{1-1/e}=\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(T^{2/3}). Tajdini et al. (2024) subsequently gave nearly minimax-optimal upper and lower bounds for a stronger regret notion based on robust-greedy maximization.

3 Problem Setting

Let V=[n]V=[n] be a ground set and let 2≤k≤n2\leq k\leq n. At each round t∈[T]t\in[T], the reward function ft:2V→[0,1]f_{t}:2^{V}\to[0,1] is monotone and submodular11 1 The upper bound of 11 is without loss of generality: if ft​(S)≤Bf_{t}(S)\leq B, ∀t∈[T],S⊆V\forall t\in[T],S\subseteq V, for some known common upper bound B>0B>0, we may replace each ftf_{t} by ft/Bf_{t}/B.. We assume that ftf_{t} is normalized, i.e., ft​(∅)=0f_{t}(\varnothing)=0. The sequence of reward functions f1,…,fTf_{1},\ldots,f_{T} is fixed in advance by an oblivious adversary, independently of the learner’s random choices.

Formally, a function ff is submodular iff for all A⊆BA\subseteq B and e∈V∖Be\in V\setminus B it holds that f⁡(A∪{e})−f⁡(A)≥f⁡(B∪{e})−f⁡(B)f(A\cup\{e\})-f(A)\geq f(B\cup\{e\})-f(B). Moreover, ff is monotone iff for all A⊆BA\subseteq B, it holds f⁡(A)≤f⁡(B)f(A)\leq f(B).

On round tt, the learner selects a possibly randomized set St⊆VS_{t}\subseteq V satisfying |St|≤k|S_{t}|\leq k and observes only the scalar value ft​(St)f_{t}(S_{t}). We measure the performance of the learner via (1−1/e)(1-1/e)-regret:

ℛT1−1/e≔(1−1/e)​max⁡∑t=1TS⊆V|S|≤k⁡ft​(S)−𝔼⁡[∑t=1Tft​(St)],\Reg_{T}^{1-1/e}\coloneqq(1-1/e)\max_{\begin{subarray}{c}S\subseteq V\\ |S|\leq k\end{subarray}}\sum_{t=1}^{T}f_{t}(S)-\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{t=1}^{T}f_{t}(S_{t})\right],

where 𝔼⁡[⋅]\mathbb{E}[\cdot] is over the learner’s random choices.

Notation. Let Δn≔{𝒑∈ℝ≥0n:∑i=1npi=1}\Delta_{n}\coloneq\left\{\bm{p}\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}^{n}:\sum_{i=1}^{n}p_{i}=1\right\} denote the probability simplex over VV. Throughout the paper, 𝔼t\mathbb{E}_{t} denotes expectation over the learner’s sampling randomness on round tt, conditional on the preceding history and the selected distribution 𝒑t\bm{p}_{t}.

4 Full-Information Setting

We begin with the full-information setting, which provides the reduction underlying our bandit algorithm. In this setting, the learner, after playing on round tt, observes the reward function ftf_{t}.

4.1 Full-information Algorithm

The learner uses an online linear optimization (OLO) algorithm to maintain a distribution 𝒑t∈Δn\bm{p}_{t}\in\Delta_{n} over the ground set. On each round, it draws kk elements independently from 𝒑t\bm{p}_{t} with replacement and plays their union StS_{t}. Repeated elements appear only once in StS_{t}, so |St|≤k|S_{t}|\leq k.

To describe the linear feedback supplied to the OLO algorithm, we first define the expected reward of mm elements sampled i.i.d. with replacement. For 𝒑∈Δn\bm{p}\in\Delta_{n}, let BmB_{m} be the union of mm independent draws from 𝒑\bm{p}, with B0≔∅B_{0}\coloneq\varnothing, and define

Ft,m​(𝒑)≔𝔼t​[ft​(Bm)].F_{t,m}(\bm{p})\coloneq\mathbb{E}_{t}[f_{t}(B_{m})].

We extend Ft,mF_{t,m} to ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} through the polynomial

Ft,m​(𝒑)≔∑(i1,…,im)∈Vmft​({i1,…,im})​∏r=1mpir.F_{t,m}(\bm{p})\coloneq\sum_{(i_{1},\ldots,i_{m})\in V^{m}}f_{t}(\{i_{1},\ldots,i_{m}\})\prod_{r=1}^{m}p_{i_{r}}.

This extension agrees with the sampling expectation on Δn\Delta_{n}; all gradients below refer to this polynomial. Setting ρ≔1−1/k\rho\coloneq 1-1/k, we use the potential

Gt​(𝒑)≔∑m=1kρk−mm​Ft,m​(𝒑).G_{t}(\bm{p})\coloneq\sum_{m=1}^{k}\frac{\rho^{k-m}}{m}F_{t,m}(\bm{p}).

The potential combines expected rewards from all draw counts up to kk. Its coefficients are chosen so that, for every 𝒑∈Δn\bm{p}\in\Delta_{n} and every set S⊆VS\subseteq V with |S|=k|S|=k, it holds that

(1−1e)​ft​(S)−Ft,k​(𝒑)≤⟨∇Gt​(𝒑),𝒑S−𝒑⟩,\left(1-\frac{1}{e}\right)f_{t}(S)-F_{t,k}(\bm{p})\leq\left\langle\nabla G_{t}(\bm{p}),\bm{p}^{S}-\bm{p}\right\rangle,

where 𝒑S\bm{p}^{S} is the uniform distribution on SS. Thus, the gap between the scaled reward of SS and the learner’s expected reward is bounded by the linear reward advantage of 𝒑S\bm{p}^{S} over 𝒑\bm{p} under ∇Gt​(𝒑)\nabla G_{t}(\bm{p}).

After observing ftf_{t}, the learner computes 𝒈t≔∇Gt​(𝒑t)\bm{g}_{t}\coloneq\nabla G_{t}(\bm{p}_{t}) and supplies the linear reward ℓ⁡(𝒑)≔⟨𝒈t,𝒑⟩\ell(\bm{p})\coloneq\langle\bm{g}_{t},\bm{p}\rangle to the OLO algorithm, which returns the next distribution 𝒑t+1\bm{p}_{t+1}. Algorithm 1 summarizes this procedure. In the next subsection, we will prove the following guarantee.

Theorem 1 (Full-information guarantee, informal).

Algorithm 1 transfers the regret bound of its OLO subroutine to (1−1/e)(1-1/e)-regret for OSM:

ℛT1−1/e≤ℛTOLO.\Reg_{T}^{1-1/e}\leq\Reg_{T}^{\mathrm{OLO}}.

In particular, an OLO algorithm with 𝒪⁡(T)\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{T}) regret yields ℛT1−1/e=𝒪⁡(T)\Reg_{T}^{1-1/e}=\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{T}) for OSM.

Discussion. This result matches the established 𝒪⁡(T)\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{T}) (1−1/e)(1-1/e)-regret rate for full-information OSM; this rate by itself is not a new contribution. Reducing OSM to OLO is also an established technique, rooted in non-oblivious potentials for offline submodular maximization (Filmus and Ward, 2014) and developed through non-oblivious boosting (Zhang et al., 2022) and upper-linearizable functions (Pedramfar and Aggarwal, 2024). Related approaches use non-oblivious potentials under bandit feedback (Wan et al., 2023) or reduce OSM to online convex optimization for WTP functions (Si Salem et al., 2024).

Our full-information algorithm uses a potential defined through sampling with replacement. This construction forms the basis of our bandit algorithm: randomizing the number of draws and choosing matching potential coefficients allows us to estimate the resulting potential’s gradient without bias from a single observed reward.

We note here that sampling with replacement can, potentially, yield sets with fewer than kk distinct elements, leaving part of the cardinality budget unused and potentially limiting practical performance, particularly in the full-information setting.

4.2 Analysis

For a set S⊆VS\subseteq V with |S|=k|S|=k, let 𝒑S∈Δn\bm{p}^{S}\in\Delta_{n} denote the uniform distribution on SS. By monotonicity, any set with |S|<k|S|<k can be padded to size kk without decreasing its reward. We first express the gradient of Ft,mF_{t,m} in terms of the reward obtained by adding a specified element to m−1m-1 independent draws.

Lemma 1 (Gradient identity).

Fix a round tt, a distribution 𝐩∈Δn\bm{p}\in\Delta_{n}, an integer m≥1m\geq 1, and an element i∈Vi\in V. Let Bm−1B_{m-1} be the union of m−1m-1 independent draws from 𝐩\bm{p}, with B0=∅B_{0}=\varnothing. Then

∂Ft,m​(𝒑)∂pi=m​𝔼t​[ft​(Bm−1∪{i})].\frac{\partial F_{t,m}(\bm{p})}{\partial p_{i}}=m\,\mathbb{E}_{t}\!\left[f_{t}(B_{m-1}\cup\{i\})\right].

Averaging this identity under 𝒑S\bm{p}^{S} and 𝒑\bm{p} and taking the difference gives the directional derivative from 𝒑\bm{p} toward 𝒑S\bm{p}^{S}.

Corollary 1 (Directional derivative identity).

Fix a round tt, a distribution 𝐩∈Δn\bm{p}\in\Delta_{n}, an integer m≥1m\geq 1, and a set S⊆VS\subseteq V with |S|=k|S|=k. Let Bm−1B_{m-1} be the union of m−1m-1 independent draws from 𝐩\bm{p}, and let ISI_{S} be uniform on SS, independently of Bm−1B_{m-1}. Then

⟨∇Ft,m​(𝒑),𝒑S−𝒑⟩=m⁡(𝔼t​[ft​(Bm−1∪{IS})]−Ft,m​(𝒑)).\left\langle\nabla F_{t,m}(\bm{p}),\bm{p}^{S}-\bm{p}\right\rangle=m\left(\mathbb{E}_{t}\!\left[f_{t}(B_{m-1}\cup\{I_{S}\})\right]-F_{t,m}(\bm{p})\right).

Monotonicity and submodularity give a lower bound on the expected reward after adding ISI_{S} in terms of ft​(S)f_{t}(S) and the current expected reward.

Lemma 2 (Submodular averaging).

Fix a round tt and let ft:2V→ℝ≥0f_{t}:2^{V}\to\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0} be monotone and submodular. Let S⊆VS\subseteq V satisfy |S|=k|S|=k, let ρ≔1−1/k\rho\coloneq 1-1/k, and let 𝐩∈Δn\bm{p}\in\Delta_{n}. For an integer m≥1m\geq 1, let Bm−1B_{m-1} be the union of m−1m-1 independent draws from 𝐩\bm{p}, and let ISI_{S} be uniform on SS, independently of Bm−1B_{m-1}. Then

𝔼t​[ft​(Bm−1∪{IS})]≥1k​ft​(S)+ρ​Ft,m−1​(𝒑).\mathbb{E}_{t}\!\left[f_{t}(B_{m-1}\cup\{I_{S}\})\right]\geq\frac{1}{k}f_{t}(S)+\rho F_{t,m-1}(\bm{p}).

Combining Corollary 1 with Lemma 2 gives, for each m∈[k]m\in[k],

⟨∇Ft,m​(𝒑),𝒑S−𝒑⟩≥m⁡(1k​ft​(S)+ρ​Ft,m−1​(𝒑)−Ft,m​(𝒑)).\left\langle\nabla F_{t,m}(\bm{p}),\bm{p}^{S}-\bm{p}\right\rangle\geq m\left(\frac{1}{k}f_{t}(S)+\rho F_{t,m-1}(\bm{p})-F_{t,m}(\bm{p})\right).

Multiplying by ρk−m/m\rho^{k-m}/m and summing over m=1,…,km=1,\ldots,k cancels the intermediate terms Ft,mF_{t,m} for 1≤m<k1\leq m<k. Dropping the remaining nonnegative term ρk​Ft,0\rho^{k}F_{t,0}, only the Ft,kF_{t,k} term survives resulting in the inequality underlying our reduction of OSM to OLO.

Lemma 3 (Linearization inequality).

Fix a round tt and let ft:2V→ℝ≥0f_{t}:2^{V}\to\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0} be monotone and submodular. Let S⊆VS\subseteq V satisfy |S|=k|S|=k, let 𝐩S\bm{p}^{S} be uniform on SS, and set ρ≔1−1/k\rho\coloneq 1-1/k and α≔1−ρk\alpha\coloneq 1-\rho^{k}. For every 𝐩∈Δn\bm{p}\in\Delta_{n},

α​ft​(S)−Ft,k​(𝒑)≤⟨∇Gt​(𝒑),𝒑S−𝒑⟩.\alpha f_{t}(S)-F_{t,k}(\bm{p})\leq\left\langle\nabla G_{t}(\bm{p}),\bm{p}^{S}-\bm{p}\right\rangle.

Since the learner’s conditional expected reward satisfies 𝔼t​[ft​(St)]=Ft,k​(𝒑t)\mathbb{E}_{t}[f_{t}(S_{t})]=F_{t,k}(\bm{p}_{t}) and α≥1−1/e\alpha\geq 1-1/e, summing the linearization inequality over rounds converts regret on linear rewards into (1−1/e)(1-1/e)-regret for the submodular rewards.

Theorem 2 (Full-information reduction of OSM to OLO).

Let V=[n]V=[n], let 2≤k≤n2\leq k\leq n, and let f1,…,fT:2V→[0,1]f_{1},\ldots,f_{T}:2^{V}\to[0,1] be normalized, monotone, submodular reward functions. Suppose the OLO algorithm in Algorithm 1 guarantees regret on linear rewards at most ℛTOLO\Reg_{T}^{\mathrm{OLO}} on the reward vectors {𝐠t=∇Gt(𝐩t)}t=1T\{\bm{g}_{t}=\nabla G_{t}(\bm{p}_{t})\}_{t=1}^{T}. Then

ℛT1−1/e≤ℛTOLO.\Reg_{T}^{1-1/e}\leq\Reg_{T}^{\mathrm{OLO}}.

Theorem 2 uses exact gradients. Under value-oracle access to the revealed function ftf_{t}, the draws already made by Algorithm 1 can instead be used to construct an unbiased gradient estimate, as described in Appendix A.7.

Instantiating Theorem 2 with the Exponential Weights algorithm, we get the following corollary.

Corollary 2 (Full-information regret with the Exponential Weights algorithm).

Under the assumptions of Theorem 2, instantiate the OLO algorithm in Algorithm 1 with the Exponential Weights algorithm over Δn\Delta_{n}. Then

ℛT1−1/e=𝒪⁡(k​T​log⁡(n/k)).\Reg_{T}^{1-1/e}=\mathcal{O}\!\left(k\sqrt{T\log(n/k)}\right).

We refer the reader to Appendix D for more details on the Exponential Weights algorithm.

5 Bandit Setting

In the bandit setting, the learner observes only ft​(St)f_{t}(S_{t}) after playing StS_{t} and therefore cannot compute the potential gradient directly. The full-information potential GtG_{t} contains terms Ft,mF_{t,m} for every m∈[k]m\in[k], including m<km<k. Always making kk draws reveals only the reward of their union, without directly revealing the rewards associated with fewer draws. To estimate all these gradient contributions from a single reward observation, we randomize the number of draws, allowing the learner to observe rewards from smaller draw counts as well.

5.1 Bandit Algorithm

As in the full-information setting, an OLO algorithm maintains a distribution 𝒑t∈Δn\bm{p}_{t}\in\Delta_{n}. On round tt, the learner samples a draw count Mt∈[k]M_{t}\in[k] from a fixed distribution 𝒒=(q1,…,qk)∈Δk\bm{q}=(q_{1},\ldots,q_{k})\in\Delta_{k}, draws MtM_{t} elements independently from 𝒑t\bm{p}_{t} with replacement, and plays their union StS_{t}. Thus, |St|≤Mt≤k|S_{t}|\leq M_{t}\leq k.

Using the expected reward Ft,mF_{t,m} defined in Section 4, the learner’s expected reward is

Ht​(𝒑)≔∑m=1kqm​Ft,m​(𝒑),𝔼t​[ft​(St)]=Ht​(𝒑t),H_{t}(\bm{p})\coloneq\sum_{m=1}^{k}q_{m}F_{t,m}(\bm{p}),\qquad\mathbb{E}_{t}[f_{t}(S_{t})]=H_{t}(\bm{p}_{t}), (1)

where 𝔼t\mathbb{E}_{t} conditions on the history and the current distribution 𝒑t\bm{p}_{t}. To account for the random draw count, we use the potential

Gt​(𝒑)≔∑m=1kam​Ft,m​(𝒑),G_{t}(\bm{p})\coloneq\sum_{m=1}^{k}a_{m}F_{t,m}(\bm{p}), (2)

whose coefficients, with ρ≔1−1/k\rho\coloneq 1-1/k, are

am≔bmm,bm≔∑ℓ=mkρℓ−m​qℓ.a_{m}\coloneq\frac{b_{m}}{m},\qquad b_{m}\coloneq\sum_{\ell=m}^{k}\rho^{\ell-m}q_{\ell}. (3)

For k≥2k\geq 2, set β≔1/e−ρk\beta\coloneq 1/e-\rho^{k} and Zk−1≔∑r=1k−1r−1/2Z_{k-1}\coloneq\sum_{r=1}^{k-1}r^{-1/2}. We choose the draw-count distribution

qm≔{βZk−1​m,1≤m<k,1−β,m=k.q_{m}\coloneq\begin{cases}\displaystyle\frac{\beta}{Z_{k-1}\sqrt{m}},&1\leq m<k,\\[6.0pt] 1-\beta,&m=k.\end{cases} (4)

Let Nt,i≔∑r=1Mt𝟏{It,r=i}N_{t,i}\coloneq\sum_{r=1}^{M_{t}}\mathbf{1}\{I_{t,r}=i\} count the occurrences of element ii among the sampled elements. The observed reward and these counts give the unbiased gradient estimator

g~t,i≔aMt​ft​(St)​Nt,iqMt​pt,i,\widetilde{g}_{t,i}\coloneq\frac{a_{M_{t}}f_{t}(S_{t})N_{t,i}}{q_{M_{t}}p_{t,i}}, (5)

which, for strictly positive 𝒑t\bm{p}_{t}, satisfies 𝔼t​[𝒈~t]=∇Gt​(𝒑t)\mathbb{E}_{t}[\widetilde{\bm{g}}_{t}]=\nabla G_{t}(\bm{p}_{t}). To preserve the positive probabilities required by its denominator, we instantiate OLO with exponential weights and use the nonpositive feedback obtained by subtracting one from the observed reward:

zt,i≔aMt​(ft​(St)−1)​Nt,iqMt​pt,i.z_{t,i}\coloneq\frac{a_{M_{t}}(f_{t}(S_{t})-1)N_{t,i}}{q_{M_{t}}p_{t,i}}. (6)

Subtracting one shifts the observed reward from [0,1][0,1] to [−1,0][-1,0], ensuring that every coordinate of 𝒛t\bm{z}_{t} is nonpositive. This nonpositivity is used in the exponential-weights analysis below. The learner supplies the linear reward ℓ⁡(𝒑)=⟨𝒛t,𝒑⟩\ell(\bm{p})=\langle\bm{z}_{t},\bm{p}\rangle to the OLO algorithm. Starting from 𝒑1=𝟏/n\bm{p}_{1}=\mathbf{1}/n, exponential weights updates the distribution as

pt+1,i=pt,i​exp⁡(η​zt,i)∑j=1npt,j​exp⁡(η​zt,j),p_{t+1,i}=\frac{p_{t,i}\exp(\eta z_{t,i})}{\sum_{j=1}^{n}p_{t,j}\exp(\eta z_{t,j})}, (7)

where η>0\eta>0 is the learning rate. The update preserves strictly positive probabilities, so the feedback in Eq. (6) remains well-defined. The analysis below shows that the reward shift preserves the expected linear comparisons needed for the regret reduction. Algorithm 2 gives the complete procedure. In the next subsection, we will prove the following result.

Theorem 3 (Bandit guarantee, informal).

For 2≤k<n2\leq k<n, against a sequence of normalized, monotone, submodular reward functions taking values in [0,1][0,1], Algorithm 2 with a suitable learning rate achieves

ℛT1−1/e=𝒪⁡(k​nT​log⁡(n/k)).\Reg_{T}^{1-1/e}=\mathcal{O}\!\left(k\sqrt{nT\log(n/k)}\right).

Computational Complexity. Computing 𝒒\bm{q} and its cumulative probabilities takes O⁡(k)O(k) preprocessing time, as does computing bm,amb_{m},a_{m} by the backward recursion in Algorithm 2. At each round, constructing the cumulative probabilities for 𝒑t\bm{p}_{t} takes O⁡(n)O(n) time, sampling at most kk elements by binary search takes O⁡(k​log⁡n)O(k\log n) time, and computing the counts, feedback, and update takes O⁡(n+k)O(n+k) time. Thus, the total running time is O⁡(n+k​log⁡n)O(n+k\log n) per round and O⁡(n+k)O(n+k) space.

Online Gradient Descent. Appendix C gives an alternative OLO instantiation using projected Online Gradient Descent (OGD). This variant operates over an ϵ\epsilon-restricted simplex with a positive lower bound on each coordinate to control the Euclidean second moment. The (1−1/e)(1-1/e)-regret guarantee is of the same 𝒪⁡(T)\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{T}) order as for Algorithm 2.

5.2 Analysis

The high-level structure of the analysis is as follows: first, we compare the expected reward Ht​(𝒑t)H_{t}(\bm{p}_{t}) with a fixed set’s reward through the gradient of the potential. Then, we estimate the gradient from the bandit feedback. Finally, we bound the regret following the analysis of the exponential-weights algorithm ((Auer et al., 2002), Appendix D).

Bandit linearization inequality. Applying Corollary 1 and Lemma 2 gives, for each m∈[k]m\in[k],

⟨∇Ft,m​(𝒑),𝒑S−𝒑⟩≥m⁡(1k​ft​(S)+ρ​Ft,m−1​(𝒑)−Ft,m​(𝒑)).\left\langle\nabla F_{t,m}(\bm{p}),\bm{p}^{S}-\bm{p}\right\rangle\geq m\left(\frac{1}{k}f_{t}(S)+\rho F_{t,m-1}(\bm{p})-F_{t,m}(\bm{p})\right).

We multiply by am=bm/ma_{m}=b_{m}/m and sum over m=1,…,km=1,\ldots,k. The terms involving the expected rewards Ft,mF_{t,m} sum to ρ​b1​Ft,0​(𝒑)−Ht​(𝒑)\rho b_{1}F_{t,0}(\bm{p})-H_{t}(\bm{p}). Dropping the term ρ​b1​Ft,0​(𝒑)\rho b_{1}F_{t,0}(\bm{p}), which is equal to 00, gives

α⁡(𝒒)​ft​(S)−Ht​(𝒑)≤⟨∇Gt​(𝒑),𝒑S−𝒑⟩,\alpha(\bm{q})f_{t}(S)-H_{t}(\bm{p})\leq\left\langle\nabla G_{t}(\bm{p}),\bm{p}^{S}-\bm{p}\right\rangle,

where α⁡(𝒒)≔1k​∑m=1kbm=∑m=1kqm​(1−ρm)\alpha(\bm{q})\coloneq\frac{1}{k}\sum_{m=1}^{k}b_{m}=\sum_{m=1}^{k}q_{m}(1-\rho^{m}). This gives the bandit counterpart of Lemma 3.

Lemma 4 (Bandit linearization inequality).

Fix a round tt and let ft:2V→ℝ≥0f_{t}:2^{V}\to\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0} be monotone and submodular. For any distribution 𝐪∈Δk\bm{q}\in\Delta_{k}, define HtH_{t}, GtG_{t}, and their coefficients by Eq. (1)–(3). For every 𝐩∈Δn\bm{p}\in\Delta_{n} and every S⊆VS\subseteq V with |S|=k|S|=k,

α⁡(𝒒)​ft​(S)−Ht​(𝒑)≤⟨∇Gt​(𝒑),𝒑S−𝒑⟩.\alpha(\bm{q})f_{t}(S)-H_{t}(\bm{p})\leq\langle\nabla G_{t}(\bm{p}),\bm{p}^{S}-\bm{p}\rangle.

We seek a distribution 𝒒\bm{q} with α⁡(𝒒)≥1−1/e\alpha(\bm{q})\geq 1-1/e. Our bandit gradient estimator also requires qm>0q_{m}>0 for every m∈[k]m\in[k]. Concentrating all mass on m=km=k recovers the full-information potential and approximation factor 1−ρk1-\rho^{k}, which exceeds the target factor by β=1/e−ρk\beta=1/e-\rho^{k}. We use this gap to allocate total mass β\beta to draw counts m<km<k according to Eq. (4), while retaining qk=1−βq_{k}=1-\beta. The next lemma verifies that this choice satisfies both requirements.

Lemma 5 (Choice of the sampling distribution).

For k≥2k\geq 2, the vector 𝐪\bm{q} in Eq. (4) is a probability distribution with qm>0q_{m}>0 for every m∈[k]m\in[k], and

α⁡(𝒒)≥1−1e+β​ρk≥1−1e,\alpha(\bm{q})\geq 1-\frac{1}{e}+\beta\rho^{k}\geq 1-\frac{1}{e},

where β=1/e−ρk\beta=1/e-\rho^{k}.

Combining these lemmas gives the comparison used in the regret reduction.

Corollary 3 (Linearization inequality for the chosen distribution).

Under the assumptions of Lemma 4, choose 𝐪∈Δk\bm{q}\in\Delta_{k} as in Eq. (4). For every 𝐩∈Δn\bm{p}\in\Delta_{n} and every S⊆VS\subseteq V with |S|=k|S|=k,

(1−1e)​ft​(S)−Ht​(𝒑)≤⟨∇Gt​(𝒑),𝒑S−𝒑⟩.\left(1-\frac{1}{e}\right)f_{t}(S)-H_{t}(\bm{p})\leq\langle\nabla G_{t}(\bm{p}),\bm{p}^{S}-\bm{p}\rangle.

Estimating the potential’s gradient from bandit feedback. The count Nt,iN_{t,i} records all positions at which element ii was drawn. Conditional on Mt=mM_{t}=m, weighting the observed reward by Nt,i/pt,iN_{t,i}/p_{t,i} therefore recovers the derivative in Lemma 1. The additional factor am/qma_{m}/q_{m} in Eq. (5) accounts for the potential coefficient and the probability of selecting that draw count.

Lemma 6 (Unbiased gradient estimator).

Let 𝐪∈Δk\bm{q}\in\Delta_{k} and 𝐩t∈Δn\bm{p}_{t}\in\Delta_{n} have strictly positive coordinates. Under the sampling rule above,

𝔼t​[ft​(St)​Nt,ipt,i|Mt=m]=∂Ft,m​(𝒑t)∂pi.\mathbb{E}_{t}\!\left[f_{t}(S_{t})\frac{N_{t,i}}{p_{t,i}}\,\middle|\,M_{t}=m\right]=\frac{\partial F_{t,m}(\bm{p}_{t})}{\partial p_{i}}.

Consequently, 𝔼t​[𝐠~t]=∇Gt​(𝐩t)\mathbb{E}_{t}[\widetilde{\bm{g}}_{t}]=\nabla G_{t}(\bm{p}_{t}).

Subtracting one from the reward makes every coordinate of 𝒛t\bm{z}_{t} nonpositive, which permits the exponential-weights bound below without imposing a uniform lower bound on the sampling probabilities. Subtracting one from the observed reward also subtracts the same constant cq≔∑m=1kbmc_{q}\coloneq\sum_{m=1}^{k}b_{m} from every coordinate of the expected feedback. Thus, the corrected estimator

𝒈^t≔𝒛t+cq​𝟏\widehat{\bm{g}}_{t}\coloneq\bm{z}_{t}+c_{q}\mathbf{1} (8)

is unbiased. The algorithm can use 𝒛t\bm{z}_{t} directly because every distribution has total mass one: for 𝒖,𝒑t∈Δn\bm{u},\bm{p}_{t}\in\Delta_{n},

⟨𝒈^t,𝒖−𝒑t⟩=⟨𝒛t+cq​𝟏,𝒖−𝒑t⟩=⟨𝒛t,𝒖−𝒑t⟩.\langle\widehat{\bm{g}}_{t},\bm{u}-\bm{p}_{t}\rangle=\langle\bm{z}_{t}+c_{q}\mathbf{1},\bm{u}-\bm{p}_{t}\rangle=\langle\bm{z}_{t},\bm{u}-\bm{p}_{t}\rangle. (9)
Lemma 7 (Expected linear feedback).

Under the assumptions of Lemma 6, the feedback in Eq. (6) satisfies 𝔼t​[𝐳t]=∇Gt​(𝐩t)−cq​𝟏\mathbb{E}_{t}[\bm{z}_{t}]=\nabla G_{t}(\bm{p}_{t})-c_{q}\mathbf{1}, and hence 𝔼t​[𝐠^t]=∇Gt​(𝐩t)\mathbb{E}_{t}[\widehat{\bm{g}}_{t}]=\nabla G_{t}(\bm{p}_{t}). For every fixed 𝐮∈Δn\bm{u}\in\Delta_{n},

𝔼t​[⟨𝒛t,𝒖−𝒑t⟩]=⟨∇Gt​(𝒑t),𝒖−𝒑t⟩.\mathbb{E}_{t}[\langle\bm{z}_{t},\bm{u}-\bm{p}_{t}\rangle]=\langle\nabla G_{t}(\bm{p}_{t}),\bm{u}-\bm{p}_{t}\rangle.

Corollary 3 compares the submodular rewards through the potential gradient, and Lemma 7 replaces that gradient by the observed feedback in expectation. As in the full-information setting, it is enough to bound regret on linear rewards against distributions 𝒑S\bm{p}^{S} that are uniform on sets of size kk.

Theorem 4 (Bandit reduction of OSM to OLO).

Let 2≤k≤n2\leq k\leq n, and let f1,…,fT:2V→[0,1]f_{1},\ldots,f_{T}:2^{V}\to[0,1] be normalized, monotone, submodular functions. Choose 𝐪\bm{q} as in Eq. (4) and use the sampling rule and feedback Eq. (6) above. Suppose the OLO algorithm produces strictly positive 𝐩t∈Δn\bm{p}_{t}\in\Delta_{n} and guarantees regret on linear rewards at most ℛTOLO\Reg_{T}^{\mathrm{OLO}} on the reward vectors {𝐳t}t=1T\{\bm{z}_{t}\}_{t=1}^{T}. Then,

ℛT1−1/e≤ℛTOLO.\Reg_{T}^{1-1/e}\leq\Reg_{T}^{\mathrm{OLO}}.

Regret of exponential weights. To apply the reduction above, we bound the regret of exponential weights on the linear rewards defined by 𝒛t\bm{z}_{t}. The bound requires control of two quantities: the expected weighted second moment of the feedback and the initial Kullback–Leibler divergence DKL(𝒑S∥𝒑1)D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\bm{p}^{S}\|\bm{p}_{1}).

We first bound the conditional expectation of ∑ipt,i​zt,i2\sum_{i}p_{t,i}z_{t,i}^{2}. Although the importance weights in 𝒛t\bm{z}_{t} can produce large coordinates when some pt,ip_{t,i} is small, this expectation admits a bound independent of 𝒑t\bm{p}_{t} using Vq≔∑m=1kbm2​(n+m−1)/(m​qm)V_{q}\coloneq\sum_{m=1}^{k}b_{m}^{2}(n+m-1)/(mq_{m}). This quantity also explains the allocation of probability among draw counts below kk: since bm≤1b_{m}\leq 1 and n+m−1≤2​nn+m-1\leq 2n, their contribution to VqV_{q} is at most 2​n​∑m<k1/(m​qm)2n\sum_{m<k}1/(mq_{m}). For fixed total mass ∑m<kqm=β\sum_{m<k}q_{m}=\beta, this upper bound is minimized by qm∝1/mq_{m}\propto 1/\sqrt{m}, as chosen in Eq. (4).

Lemma 8 (Weighted second moment).

Let 𝐪∈Δk\bm{q}\in\Delta_{k} and 𝐩t∈Δn\bm{p}_{t}\in\Delta_{n} have strictly positive coordinates, and let ftf_{t} take values in [0,1][0,1]. Then from Eq. (6),

𝔼t​[∑i=1npt,i​zt,i2]≤∑m=1kbm2​(n+m−1)m​qm=Vq.\mathbb{E}_{t}\!\left[\sum_{i=1}^{n}p_{t,i}z_{t,i}^{2}\right]\leq\sum_{m=1}^{k}\frac{b_{m}^{2}(n+m-1)}{mq_{m}}=V_{q}.

For the distribution in Eq. (4), Vq≤32​e​n​k2V_{q}\leq 32e\,nk^{2}.

The second quantity is the initial Kullback–Leibler divergence DKL(𝒑S∥𝒑1)D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\bm{p}^{S}\|\bm{p}_{1}). Since 𝒑1=𝟏/n\bm{p}_{1}=\mathbf{1}/n and 𝒑S\bm{p}^{S} is uniform on a set of size kk, this term is DKL(𝒑S∥𝒑1)=log(n/k)D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\bm{p}^{S}\|\bm{p}_{1})=\log(n/k). Combining the two terms with Theorem 4 gives the following guarantee.

Theorem 5 (Exponential-weights guarantee).

Let 2≤k<n2\leq k<n, and let f1,…,fT:2V→[0,1]f_{1},\ldots,f_{T}:2^{V}\to[0,1] be normalized, monotone, submodular functions fixed in advance by an oblivious adversary. For every η>0\eta>0, Algorithm 2 satisfies

ℛT1−1/e≤log⁡(n/k)η+η​TVq2.\Reg_{T}^{1-1/e}\leq\frac{\log(n/k)}{\eta}+\frac{\eta TV_{q}}{2}.

In particular, choosing η=2​log⁡(n/k)/(T​Vq)\eta=\sqrt{2\log(n/k)/(TV_{q})} gives ℛT1−1/e≤𝒪⁡(k​nT​log⁡(n/k)).\Reg_{T}^{1-1/e}\leq\mathcal{O}\!\left(k\sqrt{nT\log(n/k)}\right).

We refer the reader to Appendix D for more details on the Exponential Weights algorithm.

6 Experiments

We complement our theoretical results with an empirical evaluation of Sub-EW. The experiments illustrate the algorithm’s learning behavior and practical limitations.

The details of the experimental setup, i.e., the datasets, the experimental parameters, and tuning procedures are described in Appendix E. Our code and data are available on GitHub.

Datasets. We consider three monotone submodular maximization problems. Influence is a weighted influence-maximization instance. TeamFormation is a roster-selection problem with task-dependent candidate values and redundancy penalties between candidates with similar skills. Coverage is a weighted coverage problem in which elements cover features whose importance varies across tasks.

Algorithms. We compare Sub-EW (Algorithm 2) with OpaqueGreedy (Streeter and Golovin, 2008), Bandit-IG (Niazadeh et al., 2023), MSE3 (Pasteris et al., 2024), BanditMLSM (Wan et al., 2023), and Poisson-BE (Wan and Zhang, 2026). Note that MSE3 also maintains one item distribution and samples kk times with replacement. Unlike Sub-EW, it estimates the gradient of the fixed-draw expected reward, and its guarantee relies on pseudo-concavity. We also include Random, which selects a uniformly random set of exactly kk distinct elements at each round.

Metric. In all experiments, we report empirical average approximate regret (AAR). For each evaluation run, we define

AAR⁡(t):=1t​[(1−1e)​max⁡∑s=1tS⊆V,|S|≤k⁡fs​(S)−∑s=1tfs​(Ss)].\mathrm{AAR}(t):=\frac{1}{t}\left[\left(1-\frac{1}{e}\right)\max_{S\subseteq V,\;|S|\leq k}\sum_{s=1}^{t}f_{s}(S)-\sum_{s=1}^{t}f_{s}(S_{s})\right].

The comparator is the best fixed feasible set for the first tt rounds. Lower AAR values indicate better performance. We plot the pointwise mean over ten independent evaluation runs, with shaded bands indicating one sample standard deviation above and below the mean.

Results. Figure 1 shows that Sub-EW achieves lower mean final AAR than Random, Bandit-IG, BanditMLSM, and Poisson-BE across all three datasets. MSE3 achieves the lowest mean final AAR on all three datasets. OpaqueGreedy also outperforms Sub-EW on Influence and TeamFormation, whereas Sub-EW performs better on Coverage.

Discussion. MSE3 has a 𝒪~​(T)\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\sqrt{T}) regret guarantee for sum-max functions, which include all three benchmarks, whereas our guarantee holds for arbitrary monotone submodular functions. OpaqueGreedy also performs well in practice despite its weaker theoretical regret bound. Both Sub-EW and MSE3 sample with replacement, potentially leaving part of the cardinality budget unused. However, Sub-EW also randomizes the number of draws, sometimes making fewer than kk, whereas MSE3 always makes kk draws. This randomization enables estimation of the potential’s gradient, but can reduce the obtained reward. Moreover, the importance-weighted feedback (Eq. (6)) can have high variance, potentially slowing learning over finite horizons.

7 Conclusions

We achieve 𝒪⁡(k​n​T​log⁡(n/k))\mathcal{O}(k\sqrt{nT\log(n/k)}) expected (1−1/e)(1-1/e)-regret for Bandit-OSM under cardinality constraints. Our approach combines a non-oblivious potential with a randomized number of draws, enabling an unbiased estimate of its gradient from a single observed reward.

Limitations and Future Work. Despite this guarantee, our algorithm trails some baselines in practice. Designing more effective algorithms with T\sqrt{T} regret, and extending that rate to general matroids, remain open directions.

AI use statement. We used generative AI for reviewing the literature, developing our main research idea of the potential-function analysis, and improving the presentation throughout the paper. Moreover, we used it for implementing the experiments in Section 6. Finally, we used it to proofread our work and pinpoint inconsistencies and minor errors. The authors are responsible for all content of the paper.

Appendix A Full-information algorithm proofs

A.1 Proof of Lemma 1

Lemma (Restatement of Lemma 1, Gradient identity).

Fix a round tt, a distribution 𝐩∈Δn\bm{p}\in\Delta_{n}, an integer m≥1m\geq 1, and an element i∈Vi\in V. Let Bm−1B_{m-1} be the union of m−1m-1 independent draws from 𝐩\bm{p}, with B0=∅B_{0}=\varnothing. Then

∂Ft,m​(𝒑)∂pi=m​𝔼​[ft​(Bm−1∪{i})].\frac{\partial F_{t,m}(\bm{p})}{\partial p_{i}}=m\,\mathbb{E}\!\left[f_{t}(B_{m-1}\cup\{i\})\right].
Proof.

Differentiating the polynomial definition gives

∂Ft,m​(𝒑)∂pi\displaystyle\frac{\partial F_{t,m}(\bm{p})}{\partial p_{i}} =∑j1,…,jm∈Vft​({j1,…,jm})​∂∂pi​(∏r=1mpjr)\displaystyle=\sum_{j_{1},\ldots,j_{m}\in V}f_{t}(\{j_{1},\ldots,j_{m}\})\frac{\partial}{\partial p_{i}}\left(\prod_{r=1}^{m}p_{j_{r}}\right)
=∑s=1m∑(jr)r≠s∈Vm−1(∏r≠spjr)​ft​({i}∪{jr:r≠s}).\displaystyle=\sum_{s=1}^{m}\sum_{(j_{r})_{r\neq s}\in V^{m-1}}\left(\prod_{r\neq s}p_{j_{r}}\right)f_{t}\!\left(\{i\}\cup\{j_{r}:r\neq s\}\right).

For each fixed ss, the inner sum is 𝔼⁡[ft​(Bm−1∪{i})]\mathbb{E}[f_{t}(B_{m-1}\cup\{i\})]: the draw in position ss is fixed to ii, while the other m−1m-1 draws are independent samples from 𝒑\bm{p}. All mm positions therefore make the same contribution, which proves the identity. ∎

A.2 Proof of Corollary 1

Corollary (Restatement of Corollary 1, Directional derivative identity).

Fix a round tt, a distribution 𝐩∈Δn\bm{p}\in\Delta_{n}, an integer m≥1m\geq 1, and a set S⊆VS\subseteq V with |S|=k|S|=k. Let Bm−1B_{m-1} be the union of m−1m-1 independent draws from 𝐩\bm{p}, and let ISI_{S} be uniform on SS, independently of Bm−1B_{m-1}. Then

⟨∇Ft,m​(𝒑),𝒑S−𝒑⟩=m⁡(𝔼t​[ft​(Bm−1∪{IS})]−Ft,m​(𝒑)).\left\langle\nabla F_{t,m}(\bm{p}),\bm{p}^{S}-\bm{p}\right\rangle\\ =m\left(\mathbb{E}_{t}\!\left[f_{t}(B_{m-1}\cup\{I_{S}\})\right]-F_{t,m}(\bm{p})\right).
Proof.

By Lemma 1 and the definition of 𝒑S\bm{p}^{S},

⟨∇Ft,m​(𝒑),𝒑S⟩\displaystyle\left\langle\nabla F_{t,m}(\bm{p}),\bm{p}^{S}\right\rangle =mk​∑i∈S𝔼⁡[ft​(Bm−1∪{i})]\displaystyle=\frac{m}{k}\sum_{i\in S}\mathbb{E}\!\left[f_{t}(B_{m-1}\cup\{i\})\right]
=m​𝔼​[ft​(Bm−1∪{IS})].\displaystyle=m\,\mathbb{E}\!\left[f_{t}(B_{m-1}\cup\{I_{S}\})\right].

Similarly, if I∼𝒑I\sim\bm{p} independently of Bm−1B_{m-1}, then

⟨∇Ft,m​(𝒑),𝒑⟩\displaystyle\left\langle\nabla F_{t,m}(\bm{p}),\bm{p}\right\rangle =m​∑i∈Vpi​𝔼​[ft​(Bm−1∪{i})]\displaystyle=m\sum_{i\in V}p_{i}\mathbb{E}\!\left[f_{t}(B_{m-1}\cup\{i\})\right]
=m​𝔼​[ft​(Bm−1∪{I})]\displaystyle=m\,\mathbb{E}\!\left[f_{t}(B_{m-1}\cup\{I\})\right]
=m​Ft,m​(𝒑),\displaystyle=mF_{t,m}(\bm{p}),

since Bm−1∪{I}B_{m-1}\cup\{I\} has the same distribution as BmB_{m}. Subtracting the two identities proves the claim. ∎

A.3 Proof of Lemma 2

Lemma (Restatement of Lemma 2, Submodular averaging).

Fix a round tt and let ft:2V→ℝ≥0f_{t}:2^{V}\to\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0} be monotone and submodular. Let S⊆VS\subseteq V satisfy |S|=k|S|=k, let ρ≔1−1/k\rho\coloneq 1-1/k, and let 𝐩∈Δn\bm{p}\in\Delta_{n}. For an integer m≥1m\geq 1, let Bm−1B_{m-1} be the union of m−1m-1 independent draws from 𝐩\bm{p}, and let ISI_{S} be sampled uniformly from SS, independently of Bm−1B_{m-1}. Then

𝔼⁡[ft​(Bm−1∪{IS})]≥1k​ft​(S)+ρ​Ft,m−1​(𝒑).\mathbb{E}\!\left[f_{t}(B_{m-1}\cup\{I_{S}\})\right]\geq\frac{1}{k}f_{t}(S)+\rho F_{t,m-1}(\bm{p}).
Proof.

Fix B⊆VB\subseteq V. Submodularity implies

∑i∈S(ft​(B∪{i})−ft​(B))≥ft​(B∪S)−ft​(B).\sum_{i\in S}\bigl(f_{t}(B\cup\{i\})-f_{t}(B)\bigr)\geq f_{t}(B\cup S)-f_{t}(B).

Therefore, by monotonicity,

1k​∑i∈Sft​(B∪{i})\displaystyle\frac{1}{k}\sum_{i\in S}f_{t}(B\cup\{i\}) ≥(1−1k)​ft​(B)+1k​ft​(B∪S)\displaystyle\geq\left(1-\frac{1}{k}\right)f_{t}(B)+\frac{1}{k}f_{t}(B\cup S)
≥ρ​ft​(B)+1k​ft​(S).\displaystyle\geq\rho f_{t}(B)+\frac{1}{k}f_{t}(S).

Apply this inequality to B=Bm−1B=B_{m-1} and take expectation over Bm−1B_{m-1} and the independent uniform element ISI_{S}. This yields

𝔼⁡[ft​(Bm−1∪{IS})]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\!\left[f_{t}(B_{m-1}\cup\{I_{S}\})\right] =𝔼⁡[1k​∑i∈Sft​(Bm−1∪{i})]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\!\left[\frac{1}{k}\sum_{i\in S}f_{t}(B_{m-1}\cup\{i\})\right]
≥1k​ft​(S)+ρ​𝔼​[ft​(Bm−1)]\displaystyle\geq\frac{1}{k}f_{t}(S)+\rho\,\mathbb{E}[f_{t}(B_{m-1})]
=1k​ft​(S)+ρ​Ft,m−1​(𝒑).\displaystyle=\frac{1}{k}f_{t}(S)+\rho F_{t,m-1}(\bm{p}).

∎

A.4 Proof of Lemma 3

Lemma (Restatement of Lemma 3, Linearization inequality).

Fix a round tt and let ft:2V→ℝ≥0f_{t}:2^{V}\to\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0} be monotone and submodular. Let S⊆VS\subseteq V satisfy |S|=k|S|=k, let 𝐩S∈Δn\bm{p}^{S}\in\Delta_{n} be the uniform distribution on SS, and set ρ≔1−1/k\rho\coloneq 1-1/k. Then, for every 𝐩∈Δn\bm{p}\in\Delta_{n},

(1−ρk)​ft​(S)−Ft,k​(𝒑)≤⟨∇Gt​(𝒑),𝒑S−𝒑⟩.\bigl(1-\rho^{k}\bigr)f_{t}(S)-F_{t,k}(\bm{p})\leq\left\langle\nabla G_{t}(\bm{p}),\bm{p}^{S}-\bm{p}\right\rangle.
Proof.

By Corollary 1 and Lemma 2, for each m∈[k]m\in[k],

⟨∇Ft,m​(𝒑),𝒑S−𝒑⟩\displaystyle\left\langle\nabla F_{t,m}(\bm{p}),\bm{p}^{S}-\bm{p}\right\rangle ≥mk​ft​(S)+m​ρ​Ft,m−1​(𝒑)−m​Ft,m​(𝒑).\displaystyle\geq\frac{m}{k}f_{t}(S)+m\rho F_{t,m-1}(\bm{p})-mF_{t,m}(\bm{p}).

Multiplying by ρk−m/m\rho^{k-m}/m and summing over m=1,…,km=1,\ldots,k gives

⟨∇Gt​(𝒑),𝒑S−𝒑⟩≥\displaystyle\left\langle\nabla G_{t}(\bm{p}),\bm{p}^{S}-\bm{p}\right\rangle\geq{} 1k​∑m=1kρk−m​ft​(S)\displaystyle\frac{1}{k}\sum_{m=1}^{k}\rho^{k-m}f_{t}(S)
+∑m=1kρk−m+1Ft,m−1(𝒑)−∑m=1kρk−mFt,m(𝒑).\displaystyle+\sum_{m=1}^{k}\rho^{k-m+1}F_{t,m-1}(\bm{p})-\sum_{m=1}^{k}\rho^{k-m}F_{t,m}(\bm{p}).

Because Ft,0​(𝒑)=0F_{t,0}(\bm{p})=0, the last two sums telescope to −Ft,k​(𝒑)-F_{t,k}(\bm{p}). Moreover,

1k​∑m=1kρk−m=1k​∑ℓ=0k−1ρℓ=1−ρk,\frac{1}{k}\sum_{m=1}^{k}\rho^{k-m}=\frac{1}{k}\sum_{\ell=0}^{k-1}\rho^{\ell}=1-\rho^{k},

where the last equality uses 1−ρ=1/k1-\rho=1/k. Substituting these two identities proves the claim. ∎

A.5 Proof of Theorem 2

Theorem (Restatement of Theorem 2, Full-information reduction of OSM to OLO).

Let V=[n]V=[n], let 2≤k≤n2\leq k\leq n, and let f1,…,fT:2V→[0,1]f_{1},\ldots,f_{T}:2^{V}\to[0,1] be normalized, monotone, submodular reward functions. Suppose Algorithm 1 uses an OLO algorithm that for every sequence of linear reward vectors 𝐠1,…,𝐠T\bm{g}_{1},\ldots,\bm{g}_{T}, guarantees regret ℛTOLO\Reg_{T}^{\mathrm{OLO}}. When the OLO algorithm receives 𝐠t=∇Gt​(𝐩t)\bm{g}_{t}=\nabla G_{t}(\bm{p}_{t}) on every round, Algorithm 1 satisfies

ℛT1−1/e≔(1−1e)maxS⊆V:|S|≤k∑t=1Tft(S)−𝔼[∑t=1Tft(St)]≤ℛTOLO.\Reg_{T}^{1-1/e}\coloneq\left(1-\frac{1}{e}\right)\max_{S\subseteq V:\,|S|\leq k}\sum_{t=1}^{T}f_{t}(S)-\mathbb{E}\!\left[\sum_{t=1}^{T}f_{t}(S_{t})\right]\leq\Reg_{T}^{\mathrm{OLO}}.
Proof.

Set ρ≔1−1/k\rho\coloneq 1-1/k and α≔1−ρk\alpha\coloneq 1-\rho^{k}. Fix any S⊆VS\subseteq V with |S|=k|S|=k. Lemma 3 implies, on every round tt,

α​ft​(S)−Ft,k​(𝒑t)≤⟨∇Gt​(𝒑t),𝒑S−𝒑t⟩.\alpha f_{t}(S)-F_{t,k}(\bm{p}_{t})\leq\left\langle\nabla G_{t}(\bm{p}_{t}),\bm{p}^{S}-\bm{p}_{t}\right\rangle.

Summing over tt and applying the OLO guarantee with 𝒖=𝒑S\bm{u}=\bm{p}^{S} and 𝒈t=∇Gt​(𝒑t)\bm{g}_{t}=\nabla G_{t}(\bm{p}_{t}) yields

α​∑t=1Tft​(S)−∑t=1TFt,k​(𝒑t)≤ℛTOLO.\alpha\sum_{t=1}^{T}f_{t}(S)-\sum_{t=1}^{T}F_{t,k}(\bm{p}_{t})\leq\Reg_{T}^{\mathrm{OLO}}.

Conditional on the history and 𝒑t\bm{p}_{t}, the set StS_{t} is the union of kk independent draws from 𝒑t\bm{p}_{t}. Hence 𝔼t​[ft​(St)]=Ft,k​(𝒑t)\mathbb{E}_{t}[f_{t}(S_{t})]=F_{t,k}(\bm{p}_{t}). Taking expectations and using the tower property therefore gives

α​∑t=1Tft​(S)−𝔼⁡[∑t=1Tft​(St)]≤ℛTOLO.\alpha\sum_{t=1}^{T}f_{t}(S)-\mathbb{E}\!\left[\sum_{t=1}^{T}f_{t}(S_{t})\right]\leq\Reg_{T}^{\mathrm{OLO}}.

Maximizing over all SS with |S|=k|S|=k and using α=1−(1−1/k)k≥1−1/e\alpha=1-(1-1/k)^{k}\geq 1-1/e concludes the proof. ∎

A.6 Proof of Corollary 2

Corollary (Restatement of Corollary 2, Full-information regret with the Exponential Weights algorithm).

Under the assumptions of Theorem 2, instantiate the OLO algorithm in Algorithm 1 with the Exponential Weights algorithm over Δn\Delta_{n}. Then

ℛT1−1/e=𝒪⁡(k​T​log⁡(n/k)).\Reg_{T}^{1-1/e}=\mathcal{O}\!\left(k\sqrt{T\log(n/k)}\right).
Proof.

Set ρ:=1−1/k\rho:=1-1/k. By the gradient identity for Ft,mF_{t,m} and the definition of GtG_{t}, each coordinate of 𝒈t=∇Gt​(𝒑t)\bm{g}_{t}=\nabla G_{t}(\bm{p}_{t}) satisfies

gt,i=∑m=1kρk−m​𝔼​[ft​(Bt,m−1∪{i})∣𝒑t]∈[0,k],g_{t,i}=\sum_{m=1}^{k}\rho^{k-m}\mathbb{E}\!\left[f_{t}(B_{t,m-1}\cup\{i\})\mid\bm{p}_{t}\right]\in[0,k],

where Bt,m−1B_{t,m-1} is the union of m−1m-1 independent draws from 𝒑t\bm{p}_{t}. Fix S⊆VS\subseteq V with |S|=k|S|=k, and let 𝒑S\bm{p}^{S} be uniform on SS. Exponential Weights starts from 𝒑1=(1/n,…,1/n)\bm{p}_{1}=(1/n,\ldots,1/n), so

DKL(𝒑S∥𝒑1)=log(n/k).D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\bm{p}^{S}\|\bm{p}_{1})=\log(n/k).

For any η>0\eta>0, its full-information regret bound (Appendix D.1) therefore gives

∑t=1T⟨𝒈t,𝒑S−𝒑t⟩≤log⁡(n/k)η+η​k2​T8.\sum_{t=1}^{T}\langle\bm{g}_{t},\bm{p}^{S}-\bm{p}_{t}\rangle\leq\frac{\log(n/k)}{\eta}+\frac{\eta k^{2}T}{8}.

Set α:=1−ρk\alpha:=1-\rho^{k}. The comparator inequality used in the proof of Theorem 2 gives

α​∑t=1Tft​(S)−∑t=1TFt,k​(𝒑t)≤∑t=1T⟨𝒈t,𝒑S−𝒑t⟩≤log⁡(n/k)η+η​k2​T8.\alpha\sum_{t=1}^{T}f_{t}(S)-\sum_{t=1}^{T}F_{t,k}(\bm{p}_{t})\leq\sum_{t=1}^{T}\langle\bm{g}_{t},\bm{p}^{S}-\bm{p}_{t}\rangle\leq\frac{\log(n/k)}{\eta}+\frac{\eta k^{2}T}{8}.

Since 𝔼t​[ft​(St)]=Ft,k​(𝒑t)\mathbb{E}_{t}[f_{t}(S_{t})]=F_{t,k}(\bm{p}_{t}) and α≥1−1/e\alpha\geq 1-1/e, taking expectations and maximizing over SS yields

ℛT1−1/e≤log⁡(n/k)η+η​k2​T8.\Reg_{T}^{1-1/e}\leq\frac{\log(n/k)}{\eta}+\frac{\eta k^{2}T}{8}.

Choose η=8​log⁡(n/k)/(k2​T)\eta=\sqrt{8\log(n/k)/(k^{2}T)} to obtain

ℛT1−1/e≤k​T​log⁡(n/k)2.\Reg_{T}^{1-1/e}\leq k\sqrt{\frac{T\log(n/k)}{2}}.

∎

A.7 Gradient estimation

Under value-oracle access to the revealed function ftf_{t}, one can instead construct an unbiased gradient estimate from the draws already made by Algorithm 1. Let Bt,0≔∅B_{t,0}\coloneq\varnothing and Bt,r≔{It,1,…,It,r}B_{t,r}\coloneq\{I_{t,1},\ldots,I_{t,r}\} for r=1,…,k−1r=1,\ldots,k-1, and define 𝒈~t∈ℝn\widetilde{\bm{g}}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{n} coordinatewise by

g~t,i≔∑m=1kρk−m​ft​(Bt,m−1∪{i}).\widetilde{g}_{t,i}\coloneq\sum_{m=1}^{k}\rho^{k-m}f_{t}(B_{t,m-1}\cup\{i\}).

Conditional on the preceding history and 𝒑t\bm{p}_{t}, each Bt,m−1B_{t,m-1} is the union of m−1m-1 independent draws from 𝒑t\bm{p}_{t}. Lemma 1 therefore gives

𝔼t​[g~t,i]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{t}[\widetilde{g}_{t,i}] =∑m=1kρk−m​𝔼t​[ft​(Bt,m−1∪{i})]\displaystyle=\sum_{m=1}^{k}\rho^{k-m}\mathbb{E}_{t}[f_{t}(B_{t,m-1}\cup\{i\})]
=∑m=1kρk−mm​∂Ft,m​(𝒑t)∂pi\displaystyle=\sum_{m=1}^{k}\frac{\rho^{k-m}}{m}\frac{\partial F_{t,m}(\bm{p}_{t})}{\partial p_{i}}
=∂Gt​(𝒑t)∂pi.\displaystyle=\frac{\partial G_{t}(\bm{p}_{t})}{\partial p_{i}}.

The prefixes need not be independent across mm, because this calculation uses only linearity of expectation. Moreover, 0≤g~t,i≤k0\leq\widetilde{g}_{t,i}\leq k, and constructing 𝒈~t\widetilde{\bm{g}}_{t} requires at most n​knk value queries per round. Thus, an OLO algorithm with an expected regret guarantee on linear rewards may receive 𝒈~t\widetilde{\bm{g}}_{t} in place of the exact gradient, and the same regret-transfer argument applies in expectation.

Appendix B Bandit feedback algorithm proofs

B.1 Proof of Lemma 4

Lemma (Restatement of Lemma 4, Bandit linearization inequality).

Fix a round tt and let ft:2V→ℝ≥0f_{t}:2^{V}\to\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0} be monotone and submodular. For any distribution 𝐪∈Δk\bm{q}\in\Delta_{k}, define HtH_{t}, GtG_{t}, and their coefficients by Eq. (1)–(3). For every 𝐩∈Δn\bm{p}\in\Delta_{n} and every S⊆VS\subseteq V with |S|=k|S|=k,

α⁡(𝒒)​ft​(S)−Ht​(𝒑)≤⟨∇Gt​(𝒑),𝒑S−𝒑⟩.\alpha(\bm{q})f_{t}(S)-H_{t}(\bm{p})\leq\langle\nabla G_{t}(\bm{p}),\bm{p}^{S}-\bm{p}\rangle.
Proof.

The gradient identity and submodular averaging inequality from the full-information analysis give, for each m∈[k]m\in[k],

⟨∇Ft,m​(𝒑),𝒑S−𝒑⟩≥mk​ft​(S)+m​ρ​Ft,m−1​(𝒑)−m​Ft,m​(𝒑).\langle\nabla F_{t,m}(\bm{p}),\bm{p}^{S}-\bm{p}\rangle\geq\frac{m}{k}f_{t}(S)+m\rho F_{t,m-1}(\bm{p})-mF_{t,m}(\bm{p}).

Multiplying by bm/mb_{m}/m and summing over mm yields

⟨∇Gt​(𝒑),𝒑S−𝒑⟩≥1k​∑m=1kbm​ft​(S)+∑m=1kbm​(ρ​Ft,m−1​(𝒑)−Ft,m​(𝒑)).\langle\nabla G_{t}(\bm{p}),\bm{p}^{S}-\bm{p}\rangle\geq\frac{1}{k}\sum_{m=1}^{k}b_{m}f_{t}(S)+\sum_{m=1}^{k}b_{m}\bigl(\rho F_{t,m-1}(\bm{p})-F_{t,m}(\bm{p})\bigr).

Using Ft,0=0F_{t,0}=0, bk+1=0b_{k+1}=0, and bm=qm+ρ​bm+1b_{m}=q_{m}+\rho b_{m+1}, the last sum is

∑m=1k(ρ​bm+1−bm)​Ft,m​(𝒑)=−Ht​(𝒑).\sum_{m=1}^{k}(\rho b_{m+1}-b_{m})F_{t,m}(\bm{p})=-H_{t}(\bm{p}).

Also, changing the order of summation gives

1k​∑m=1kbm=∑ℓ=1kqℓ​(1k​∑m=1ℓρℓ−m)=∑ℓ=1kqℓ​(1−ρℓ)=α⁡(𝒒).\frac{1}{k}\sum_{m=1}^{k}b_{m}=\sum_{\ell=1}^{k}q_{\ell}\left(\frac{1}{k}\sum_{m=1}^{\ell}\rho^{\ell-m}\right)=\sum_{\ell=1}^{k}q_{\ell}(1-\rho^{\ell})=\alpha(\bm{q}).

Substituting these identities proves the claim. ∎

B.2 Proof of Corollary 3

Corollary (Restatement of Corollary 3, Linearization inequality for the chosen distribution).

Under the assumptions of Lemma 4, choose 𝐪∈Δk\bm{q}\in\Delta_{k} as in Eq. (4). For every 𝐩∈Δn\bm{p}\in\Delta_{n} and every S⊆VS\subseteq V with |S|=k|S|=k,

(1−1e)​ft​(S)−Ht​(𝒑)≤⟨∇Gt​(𝒑),𝒑S−𝒑⟩.\left(1-\frac{1}{e}\right)f_{t}(S)-H_{t}(\bm{p})\leq\langle\nabla G_{t}(\bm{p}),\bm{p}^{S}-\bm{p}\rangle.
Proof.

Apply Lemmas 4 and 5, using ft​(S)≥0f_{t}(S)\geq 0. ∎

B.3 Proof of Lemma 6

Lemma (Restatement of Lemma 6, Unbiased gradient estimator).

Let 𝐪∈Δk\bm{q}\in\Delta_{k} have strictly positive coordinates, and let 𝐩t∈Δn\bm{p}_{t}\in\Delta_{n} be strictly positive. Under the sampling rule above,

𝔼t​[ft​(St)​Nt,ipt,i|Mt=m]=∂Ft,m​(𝒑t)∂pi.\mathbb{E}_{t}\!\left[f_{t}(S_{t})\frac{N_{t,i}}{p_{t,i}}\,\middle|\,M_{t}=m\right]=\frac{\partial F_{t,m}(\bm{p}_{t})}{\partial p_{i}}.

Consequently, 𝔼t​[𝐠~t]=∇Gt​(𝐩t).\mathbb{E}_{t}[\widetilde{\bm{g}}_{t}]=\nabla G_{t}(\bm{p}_{t}).

Proof.

Expanding Nt,iN_{t,i} and conditioning on each draw gives

𝔼t​[ft​(St)​Nt,ipt,i|Mt=m]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{t}\!\left[f_{t}(S_{t})\frac{N_{t,i}}{p_{t,i}}\,\middle|\,M_{t}=m\right] =∑r=1m𝔼t[ft(St)∣Mt=m,It,r=i]\displaystyle=\sum_{r=1}^{m}\mathbb{E}_{t}[f_{t}(S_{t})\mid M_{t}=m,\ I_{t,r}=i]
=m​𝔼​[ft​(Bm−1∪{i})]\displaystyle=m\,\mathbb{E}[f_{t}(B_{m-1}\cup\{i\})]
=∂Ft,m​(𝒑t)∂pi,\displaystyle=\frac{\partial F_{t,m}(\bm{p}_{t})}{\partial p_{i}},

where Bm−1B_{m-1} is the union of the remaining m−1m-1 independent draws from 𝒑t\bm{p}_{t}. The last equality is Lemma 1. Multiplying by am/qma_{m}/q_{m} and averaging over MtM_{t} proves the second claim. ∎

B.4 Proof of Lemma 7

Lemma (Restatement of Lemma 7, Expected linear feedback).

Under the assumptions of Lemma 6, the feedback in Eq. (6) satisfies 𝔼t​[𝐳t]=∇Gt​(𝐩t)−cq​𝟏\mathbb{E}_{t}[\bm{z}_{t}]=\nabla G_{t}(\bm{p}_{t})-c_{q}\mathbf{1}, and hence 𝔼t​[𝐠^t]=∇Gt​(𝐩t)\mathbb{E}_{t}[\widehat{\bm{g}}_{t}]=\nabla G_{t}(\bm{p}_{t}). For every fixed 𝐮∈Δn\bm{u}\in\Delta_{n},

𝔼t​[⟨𝒛t,𝒖−𝒑t⟩]=⟨∇Gt​(𝒑t),𝒖−𝒑t⟩.\mathbb{E}_{t}[\langle\bm{z}_{t},\bm{u}-\bm{p}_{t}\rangle]=\langle\nabla G_{t}(\bm{p}_{t}),\bm{u}-\bm{p}_{t}\rangle.

Since 𝔼t​[Nt,i∣Mt=m]=m​pt,i\mathbb{E}_{t}[N_{t,i}\mid M_{t}=m]=mp_{t,i},

𝔼t​[g~t,i−zt,i]=∑m=1kam​m=cq.\mathbb{E}_{t}[\widetilde{g}_{t,i}-z_{t,i}]=\sum_{m=1}^{k}a_{m}m=c_{q}.

The first claim follows from Lemma 6. The second uses ⟨𝟏,𝒖−𝒑t⟩=0\langle\mathbf{1},\bm{u}-\bm{p}_{t}\rangle=0. ∎

B.5 Proof of Lemma 5

Lemma (Restatement of Lemma 5, Choice of the sampling distribution).

Let k≥2k\geq 2, ρ≔1−1/k\rho\coloneq 1-1/k, β≔1/e−ρk\beta\coloneq 1/e-\rho^{k}, Zk−1≔∑r=1k−1r−1/2Z_{k-1}\coloneq\sum_{r=1}^{k-1}r^{-1/2} and define

qm≔{βZk−1​m,1≤m<k,1−β,m=k.q_{m}\coloneq\begin{cases}\displaystyle\frac{\beta}{Z_{k-1}\sqrt{m}},&1\leq m<k,\\[6.0pt] 1-\beta,&m=k.\end{cases}

Then 𝐪\bm{q} is a probability distribution with qm>0q_{m}>0 for every m∈[k]m\in[k], and

α⁡(𝒒)≔∑m=1kqm​(1−ρm)≥1−1/e+β​ρk≥1−1e.\alpha(\bm{q})\coloneq\sum_{m=1}^{k}q_{m}(1-\rho^{m})\geq 1-1/e+\beta\rho^{k}\geq 1-\frac{1}{e}.
Proof.

Since k≥2k\geq 2 and ρ=1−1/k\rho=1-1/k, we have 0<ρk<1/e0<\rho^{k}<1/e and hence 0<β<10<\beta<1. Every qmq_{m} is positive, and

∑m=1k−1qm=βZk−1​∑m=1k−11m=β.\sum_{m=1}^{k-1}q_{m}=\frac{\beta}{Z_{k-1}}\sum_{m=1}^{k-1}\frac{1}{\sqrt{m}}=\beta.

Together with qk=1−βq_{k}=1-\beta, this shows that the probabilities sum to one. Since every 1−ρm1-\rho^{m} is nonnegative,

α⁡(𝒒)=∑m=1kqm​(1−ρm)≥(1−β)​(1−ρk)=1−1e+β​ρk≥1−1e,\alpha(\bm{q})=\sum_{m=1}^{k}q_{m}(1-\rho^{m})\geq(1-\beta)(1-\rho^{k})=1-\frac{1}{e}+\beta\rho^{k}\geq 1-\frac{1}{e},

where the equality uses β+ρk=1/e\beta+\rho^{k}=1/e. ∎

B.6 Proof of Theorem 4

Theorem (Restatement of Theorem 4, Bandit reduction of OSM to OLO).

Let 2≤k≤n2\leq k\leq n, and let f1,…,fT:2V→[0,1]f_{1},\ldots,f_{T}:2^{V}\to[0,1] be normalized, monotone, submodular functions. Choose 𝐪\bm{q} as in Eq. (4) and use the sampling rule and feedback Eq. (6) above. Suppose the OLO algorithm produces strictly positive 𝐩t∈Δn\bm{p}_{t}\in\Delta_{n} and guarantees regret on linear rewards at most ℛTOLO\Reg_{T}^{\mathrm{OLO}} on the reward vectors {𝐳t}t=1T\{\bm{z}_{t}\}_{t=1}^{T}. Then,

ℛT1−1/e≤ℛTOLO.\Reg_{T}^{1-1/e}\leq\Reg_{T}^{\mathrm{OLO}}.
Proof.

Fix S⊆VS\subseteq V with |S|=k|S|=k. By Corollary 3, 𝔼t​[ft​(St)]=Ht​(𝒑t)\mathbb{E}_{t}[f_{t}(S_{t})]=H_{t}(\bm{p}_{t}), and Lemma 7,

(1−1e)​ft​(S)−𝔼t​[ft​(St)]≤𝔼t​[⟨𝒛t,𝒑S−𝒑t⟩].\left(1-\frac{1}{e}\right)f_{t}(S)-\mathbb{E}_{t}[f_{t}(S_{t})]\leq\mathbb{E}_{t}[\langle\bm{z}_{t},\bm{p}^{S}-\bm{p}_{t}\rangle].

Maximizing over SS concludes the proof. ∎

B.7 Proof of Lemma 8

Lemma (Restatement of Lemma 8, Weighted second moment).

Let 𝐪∈Δk\bm{q}\in\Delta_{k} and 𝐩t∈Δn\bm{p}_{t}\in\Delta_{n} have strictly positive coordinates, and let ftf_{t} take values in [0,1][0,1]. Then from Eq. (6),

𝔼t​[∑i=1npt,i​zt,i2]≤∑m=1kbm2​(n+m−1)m​qm=Vq.\mathbb{E}_{t}\!\left[\sum_{i=1}^{n}p_{t,i}z_{t,i}^{2}\right]\leq\sum_{m=1}^{k}\frac{b_{m}^{2}(n+m-1)}{mq_{m}}=V_{q}.

𝔼t​[Nt,i2∣Mt=m]=m​pt,i+m⁡(m−1)​pt,i2.\mathbb{E}_{t}[N_{t,i}^{2}\mid M_{t}=m]=mp_{t,i}+m(m-1)p_{t,i}^{2}.

𝔼t​[∑i=1npt,i​zt,i2]≤∑m=1kam2qm​m​(n+m−1)=Vq.\mathbb{E}_{t}\!\left[\sum_{i=1}^{n}p_{t,i}z_{t,i}^{2}\right]\leq\sum_{m=1}^{k}\frac{a_{m}^{2}}{q_{m}}m(n+m-1)=V_{q}.

For the chosen distribution, bm≤∑ℓ=mkqℓ≤1b_{m}\leq\sum_{\ell=m}^{k}q_{\ell}\leq 1 and bk=qk=1−βb_{k}=q_{k}=1-\beta. Therefore,

Vq\displaystyle V_{q} ≤(n+k−1)​(∑m=1k−11m​qm+1−βk)\displaystyle\leq(n+k-1)\left(\sum_{m=1}^{k-1}\frac{1}{mq_{m}}+\frac{1-\beta}{k}\right)
=(n+k−1)​(Zk−12β+1−βk).\displaystyle=(n+k-1)\left(\frac{Z_{k-1}^{2}}{\beta}+\frac{1-\beta}{k}\right).

Zk−12=(∑m=1k−1qm​1m​qm)2≤β​∑m=1k−11m​qm.Z_{k-1}^{2}=\left(\sum_{m=1}^{k-1}\sqrt{q_{m}}\,\frac{1}{\sqrt{mq_{m}}}\right)^{2}\leq\beta\sum_{m=1}^{k-1}\frac{1}{mq_{m}}.
