β=1e−ρk≥1e(1−e−1/(2k))≥14​e​k,\beta=\frac{1}{e}-\rho^{k}\geq\frac{1}{e}(1-e^{-1/(2k)})\geq\frac{1}{4ek},

using 1−e−x≥x/21-e^{-x}\geq x/2 for 0≤x≤10\leq x\leq 1. It follows that

Vq≤(n+k−1)​(16​e​k​(k−1)+1k)≤16​e​k2​(n+k−1)≤32​e​n​k2.V_{q}\leq(n+k-1)\left(16e\,k(k-1)+\frac{1}{k}\right)\leq 16e\,k^{2}(n+k-1)\leq 32e\,nk^{2}.

∎

B.8 Proof of Theorem 5

Theorem (Restatement of Theorem 5, Exponential-weights guarantee).

Let 2≤k<n2\leq k<n, and let f1,…,fT:2V→[0,1]f_{1},\ldots,f_{T}:2^{V}\to[0,1] be normalized, monotone, submodular functions fixed in advance by an oblivious adversary. For every η>0\eta>0, Algorithm 2 satisfies

ℛT1−1/e≤log⁡(n/k)η+η​TVq2.\Reg_{T}^{1-1/e}\leq\frac{\log(n/k)}{\eta}+\frac{\eta TV_{q}}{2}.

In particular, choosing η=2​log⁡(n/k)/(T​Vq)\eta=\sqrt{2\log(n/k)/(TV_{q})} gives

ℛT1−1/e≤𝒪⁡(k​nT​log⁡(n/k)).\Reg_{T}^{1-1/e}\leq\mathcal{O}\!\left(k\sqrt{nT\log(n/k)}\right).
Proof.

We use the second-order exponential-weights bound with a distributional comparator 𝒖∈Δn\bm{u}\in\Delta_{n}. For completeness, define

DKL(𝒖∥𝒗)≔∑i:ui>0uiloguivi,Wt≔∑i=1npt,iexp(ηzt,i).D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\bm{u}\|\bm{v})\coloneq\sum_{i:u_{i}>0}u_{i}\log\frac{u_{i}}{v_{i}},\qquad W_{t}\coloneq\sum_{i=1}^{n}p_{t,i}\exp(\eta z_{t,i}).

The update gives

DKL(𝒖∥𝒑t+1)−DKL(𝒖∥𝒑t)=logWt−η⟨𝒛t,𝒖⟩.D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\bm{u}\|\bm{p}_{t+1})-D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\bm{u}\|\bm{p}_{t})=\log W_{t}-\eta\langle\bm{z}_{t},\bm{u}\rangle.

Since zt,i≤0z_{t,i}\leq 0, the inequalities ex≤1+x+x2/2e^{x}\leq 1+x+x^{2}/2 for x≤0x\leq 0 and log⁡x≤x−1\log x\leq x-1 give

log⁡Wt≤η⁡⟨𝒛t,𝒑t⟩+η22​∑i=1npt,i​zt,i2.\log W_{t}\leq\eta\langle\bm{z}_{t},\bm{p}_{t}\rangle+\frac{\eta^{2}}{2}\sum_{i=1}^{n}p_{t,i}z_{t,i}^{2}.

Rearranging, summing over tt, and using nonnegativity of KL divergence yields

∑t=1T⟨𝒛t,𝒖−𝒑t⟩≤DKL(𝒖∥𝒑1)η+η2​∑t=1T∑i=1npt,i​zt,i2.\sum_{t=1}^{T}\langle\bm{z}_{t},\bm{u}-\bm{p}_{t}\rangle\leq\frac{D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\bm{u}\|\bm{p}_{1})}{\eta}+\frac{\eta}{2}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\sum_{i=1}^{n}p_{t,i}z_{t,i}^{2}.

This is the KL-divergence form of the second-order exponential-weights analysis; see also [Hazan, 2016, Theorem 1.5]. The inequality holds for every realization of the feedback and every η>0\eta>0.

For a set SS of size kk, 𝒑S\bm{p}^{S} is uniform on SS and 𝒑1\bm{p}_{1} is uniform on VV, so

DKL(𝒑S∥𝒑1)=∑i∈S1klog1/k1/n=log(n/k).D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\bm{p}^{S}\|\bm{p}_{1})=\sum_{i\in S}\frac{1}{k}\log\frac{1/k}{1/n}=\log(n/k).

Taking expectations and applying Lemma 8 therefore gives, for every such SS,

𝔼⁡[∑t=1T⟨𝒛t,𝒑S−𝒑t⟩]≤log⁡(n/k)η+η​T​Vq2.\mathbb{E}\!\left[\sum_{t=1}^{T}\langle\bm{z}_{t},\bm{p}^{S}-\bm{p}_{t}\rangle\right]\leq\frac{\log(n/k)}{\eta}+\frac{\eta TV_{q}}{2}.

Apply Theorem 4 to obtain the first claim. With the stated learning rate, the bound becomes 2​T​Vq​log⁡(n/k)\sqrt{2TV_{q}\log(n/k)}; the estimate Vq≤32​e​n​k2V_{q}\leq 32e\,nk^{2} from Lemma 8 gives the second claim. ∎

Appendix C A Projected OGD Variant

This appendix gives an alternative Euclidean instantiation of the bandit reduction. We keep qq, ama_{m}, bmb_{m}, ρ\rho, and β\beta from the main section, and use the same sampling rule and feedback vector ztz_{t} from Eq. (6). Unlike exponential weights, the Euclidean analysis needs a uniform bound on inverse coordinate probabilities. We therefore work on a restricted simplex.

C.1 Restriction and the smoothed comparator

Set

ϵ0≔β​ρk,K≔Δnϵ0≔{p∈Δn:pi≥ϵ0/n​ for all ​i∈V}.\epsilon_{0}\coloneq\beta\rho^{k},\qquad K\coloneq\Delta_{n}^{\epsilon_{0}}\coloneq\{p\in\Delta_{n}:p_{i}\geq\epsilon_{0}/n\text{ for all }i\in V\}.

For S⊆VS\subseteq V with |S|=k|S|=k, define

pS,ϵ0≔(1−ϵ0)​pS+ϵ0​𝟏n∈K.p^{S,\epsilon_{0}}\coloneq(1-\epsilon_{0})p^{S}+\epsilon_{0}\frac{\mathbf{1}}{n}\in K.

We first show that smoothing still permits the target benchmark.

Lemma 9 (Smoothed linearization inequality).

For any ϵ∈[0,1)\epsilon\in[0,1), let pS,ϵ≔(1−ϵ)​pS+ϵ​𝟏/np^{S,\epsilon}\coloneq(1-\epsilon)p^{S}+\epsilon\mathbf{1}/n. For every p∈Δnp\in\Delta_{n},

(1−ϵ)​α​(q)​ft​(S)−Ht​(p)≤⟨∇Gt​(p),pS,ϵ−p⟩.(1-\epsilon)\alpha(q)f_{t}(S)-H_{t}(p)\leq\langle\nabla G_{t}(p),p^{S,\epsilon}-p\rangle.

For the choices of qq and ϵ0\epsilon_{0} above, (1−ϵ0)​α​(q)≥1−1/e(1-\epsilon_{0})\alpha(q)\geq 1-1/e.

Proof.

For every set BB, submodular averaging and monotonicity give

∑ipiS,ϵ​ft​(B∪{i})\displaystyle\sum_{i}p_{i}^{S,\epsilon}f_{t}(B\cup\{i\}) ≥(1−ϵ)​(1k​ft​(S)+ρ​ft​(B))+ϵ​ft​(B)\displaystyle\geq(1-\epsilon)\left(\frac{1}{k}f_{t}(S)+\rho f_{t}(B)\right)+\epsilon f_{t}(B)
=1−ϵk​ft​(S)+(ρ+ϵk)​ft​(B).\displaystyle=\frac{1-\epsilon}{k}f_{t}(S)+\left(\rho+\frac{\epsilon}{k}\right)f_{t}(B).

Using the gradient identity and summing with weights am=bm/ma_{m}=b_{m}/m, the same cancellation as in Lemma 4 yields

⟨∇Gt​(p),pS,ϵ−p⟩≥\displaystyle\langle\nabla G_{t}(p),p^{S,\epsilon}-p\rangle\geq{} (1−ϵ)​α​(q)​ft​(S)−Ht​(p)\displaystyle(1-\epsilon)\alpha(q)f_{t}(S)-H_{t}(p)
+ϵk∑m=1kbmFt,m−1(p).\displaystyle+\frac{\epsilon}{k}\sum_{m=1}^{k}b_{m}F_{t,m-1}(p).

The last term is nonnegative. For the coefficient, Lemma 5 gives α⁡(q)≥1−1/e+ϵ0\alpha(q)\geq 1-1/e+\epsilon_{0}. Since α⁡(q)≤1\alpha(q)\leq 1,

(1−ϵ0)​α​(q)≥α⁡(q)−ϵ0≥1−1e.(1-\epsilon_{0})\alpha(q)\geq\alpha(q)-\epsilon_{0}\geq 1-\frac{1}{e}.

Also 0<ϵ0<10<\epsilon_{0}<1, so KK is nonempty and contains the uniform distribution. ∎

Combining the lemma with 𝔼t​[ft​(St)]=Ht​(pt)\mathbb{E}_{t}[f_{t}(S_{t})]=H_{t}(p_{t}) and Lemma 7, for iterates in KK we obtain

(1−1e)​ft​(S)−𝔼t​[ft​(St)]≤𝔼t​[⟨zt,pS,ϵ0−pt⟩].\left(1-\frac{1}{e}\right)f_{t}(S)-\mathbb{E}_{t}[f_{t}(S_{t})]\leq\mathbb{E}_{t}[\langle z_{t},p^{S,\epsilon_{0}}-p_{t}\rangle]. (10)

The restriction is independent of TT: its cost is absorbed by the approximation coefficient rather than by an additive per-round error.

C.2 Algorithm and Euclidean second moment

Initialize p1=𝟏/np_{1}=\mathbf{1}/n. On each round, sample MtM_{t}, the draws, and the feedback ztz_{t} exactly as in Algorithm 2, but replace its exponential-weights update by

pt+1≔ΠK​(pt+η​zt),p_{t+1}\coloneq\Pi_{K}(p_{t}+\eta z_{t}), (11)

where ΠK\Pi_{K} is Euclidean projection onto KK. This is projected gradient ascent on the linear reward ⟨zt,p⟩\langle z_{t},p\rangle, or equivalently OGD on the linear loss −⟨zt,p⟩-\langle z_{t},p\rangle. Using g^t=zt+cq​𝟏\widehat{g}_{t}=z_{t}+c_{q}\mathbf{1} gives the same projection, since every point of KK has coordinate sum one.

Lemma 10 (Euclidean second moment).

If pt∈Kp_{t}\in K, then

𝔼t​[‖zt‖22]≤n​Vqϵ0.\mathbb{E}_{t}[\|z_{t}\|_{2}^{2}]\leq\frac{nV_{q}}{\epsilon_{0}}.
Proof.

The coordinate floor gives, pointwise,

∑izt,i2≤nϵ0​∑ipt,i​zt,i2.\sum_{i}z_{t,i}^{2}\leq\frac{n}{\epsilon_{0}}\sum_{i}p_{t,i}z_{t,i}^{2}.

Take conditional expectations and apply Lemma 8. ∎

C.3 Regret guarantee

Theorem 6 (Projected OGD guarantee).

Under the setting of the main bandit section, the projected OGD variant above satisfies, for every η>0\eta>0,

ℛT1−1/e≤12​k​η+η​nTVq2​ϵ0.\Reg_{T}^{1-1/e}\leq\frac{1}{2k\eta}+\frac{\eta nTV_{q}}{2\epsilon_{0}}.

In particular, choosing η=ϵ0/(k​n​T​Vq)\eta=\sqrt{\epsilon_{0}/(knTV_{q})} gives

ℛT1−1/e≤nTVqk​ϵ0=𝒪⁡(nk​T).\Reg_{T}^{1-1/e}\leq\sqrt{\frac{nTV_{q}}{k\epsilon_{0}}}=\mathcal{O}\!\left(nk\sqrt{T}\right).
Proof.

For every u∈Ku\in K, nonexpansiveness of Euclidean projection gives

‖pt+1−u‖22\displaystyle\|p_{t+1}-u\|_{2}^{2} ≤‖pt+η​zt−u‖22\displaystyle\leq\|p_{t}+\eta z_{t}-u\|_{2}^{2}
=‖pt−u‖22−2​η​⟨zt,u−pt⟩+η2​‖zt‖22.\displaystyle=\|p_{t}-u\|_{2}^{2}-2\eta\langle z_{t},u-p_{t}\rangle+\eta^{2}\|z_{t}\|_{2}^{2}.

Rearranging, summing, and dropping the final squared distance yields

∑t=1T⟨zt,u−pt⟩≤‖u−p1‖222​η+η2​∑t=1T‖zt‖22.\sum_{t=1}^{T}\langle z_{t},u-p_{t}\rangle\leq\frac{\|u-p_{1}\|_{2}^{2}}{2\eta}+\frac{\eta}{2}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\|z_{t}\|_{2}^{2}.

Taking expectations and applying Lemma 10,

𝔼⁡[∑t=1T⟨zt,u−pt⟩]≤‖u−p1‖222​η+η​n​T​Vq2​ϵ0.\mathbb{E}\!\left[\sum_{t=1}^{T}\langle z_{t},u-p_{t}\rangle\right]\leq\frac{\|u-p_{1}\|_{2}^{2}}{2\eta}+\frac{\eta nTV_{q}}{2\epsilon_{0}}.

For u=pS,ϵ0u=p^{S,\epsilon_{0}} and p1=𝟏/np_{1}=\mathbf{1}/n,

‖u−p1‖22=(1−ϵ0)2​(1k−1n)≤1k.\|u-p_{1}\|_{2}^{2}=(1-\epsilon_{0})^{2}\left(\frac{1}{k}-\frac{1}{n}\right)\leq\frac{1}{k}.

Taking expectations and summing Eq. (10) therefore proves the claimed regret bound for every fixed SS of size kk. Maximizing over SS and optimizing in η\eta gives the explicit square-root guarantee.

The main proof established Vq=𝒪⁡(n​k2)V_{q}=\mathcal{O}(nk^{2}) and β−1=𝒪⁡(k)\beta^{-1}=\mathcal{O}(k). Moreover, log(1−x)≥−x/(1−x)\log(1-x)\geq-x/(1-x) for 0≤x<10\leq x<1 implies

ρk≥exp⁡(−kk−1)≥e−2.\rho^{k}\geq\exp\!\left(-\frac{k}{k-1}\right)\geq e^{-2}.

Thus ϵ0−1=(β​ρk)−1=𝒪⁡(k)\epsilon_{0}^{-1}=(\beta\rho^{k})^{-1}=\mathcal{O}(k), which gives the stated dependence on n,k,Tn,k,T. ∎

Computational complexity.

Write d≔ϵ0/nd\coloneq\epsilon_{0}/n. The projection has the form

[ΠK​(v)]i=max⁡{d,vi−τ},∑imax⁡{d,vi−τ}=1,[\Pi_{K}(v)]_{i}=\max\{d,v_{i}-\tau\},\qquad\sum_{i}\max\{d,v_{i}-\tau\}=1,

where the threshold τ\tau can be found by sorting the coordinates. This takes O⁡(n​log⁡n)O(n\log n) time. Including the sampling and estimator construction, the OGD variant takes O⁡(n​log⁡n)O(n\log n) time per round because k≤nk\leq n, and O⁡(n+k)O(n+k) storage, in the same arithmetic model as the main algorithm.

Appendix D The Exponential Weights Algorithm

Exponential weights maintains a distribution 𝒑t∈Δn\bm{p}_{t}\in\Delta_{n} over n≥2n\geq 2 coordinates, assigning greater probability to coordinates with larger cumulative feedback. Starting from 𝒑1=𝟏/n\bm{p}_{1}=\boldsymbol{1}/n, it uses learning rate η>0\eta>0 and updates

pt+1,i=pt,i​exp⁡(η​vt,i)∑j=1npt,j​exp⁡(η​vt,j).p_{t+1,i}=\frac{p_{t,i}\exp(\eta v_{t,i})}{\sum_{j=1}^{n}p_{t,j}\exp(\eta v_{t,j})}. (12)

The feedback 𝒗t\bm{v}_{t} depends on the observation model. For a fixed distribution 𝒖∈Δn\bm{u}\in\Delta_{n}, write DKL(𝒖∥𝒑):=∑i:ui>0uilog(ui/pi)D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\bm{u}\|\bm{p}):=\sum_{i:u_{i}>0}u_{i}\log(u_{i}/p_{i}). All logarithms are natural.

D.1 Full-information feedback

After choosing 𝒑t\bm{p}_{t}, the learner observes the entire reward vector 𝒈t∈[0,B]n\bm{g}_{t}\in[0,B]^{n}, where B>0B>0, and sets 𝒗t=𝒈t\bm{v}_{t}=\bm{g}_{t}. Its linear reward is ⟨𝒈t,𝒑t⟩\langle\bm{g}_{t},\bm{p}_{t}\rangle. This is the Hedge algorithm; see Hazan [2016](Section 1.3.3). We state the standard regret bound in its Hoeffding-lemma form.

Theorem 7 (Full-information regret).

For any sequence 𝐠t∈[0,B]n\bm{g}_{t}\in[0,B]^{n} and any η>0\eta>0, exponential weights satisfies, for every fixed distribution 𝐮∈Δn\bm{u}\in\Delta_{n},

∑t=1T⟨𝒈t,𝒖−𝒑t⟩≤DKL(𝒖∥𝒑1)η+η​B2​T8.\sum_{t=1}^{T}\langle\bm{g}_{t},\bm{u}-\bm{p}_{t}\rangle\leq\frac{D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\bm{u}\|\bm{p}_{1})}{\eta}+\frac{\eta B^{2}T}{8}. (13)

Since DKL(𝐮∥𝐩1)≤lognD_{\mathrm{KL}}(\bm{u}\|\bm{p}_{1})\leq\log n, choosing η=8​log⁡n/(B2​T)\eta=\sqrt{8\log n/(B^{2}T)} bounds regret against the best fixed action by B​T​log⁡n/2B\sqrt{T\log n/2}. This is also the bound against the best fixed distribution, since rewards are linear.

Our full-information reduction uses 𝒈t=∇Gt​(𝒑t)∈[0,k]n\bm{g}_{t}=\nabla G_{t}(\bm{p}_{t})\in[0,k]^{n}; setting B=kB=k recovers the guarantee in the main text.

D.2 Bandit feedback

With bandit feedback, the learner observes only the reward of its sampled action and constructs an importance-weighted estimate. This is the principle underlying Exp3, introduced by Auer et al. [2002]. We use the loss-based formulation described by Hazan [2016](Section 6.2.1), expressed as nonpositive rewards. For example, when It∼𝒑tI_{t}\sim\bm{p}_{t} and only gt,It∈[0,B]g_{t,I_{t}}\in[0,B] is observed, set 𝒗t=𝒛t\bm{v}_{t}=\bm{z}_{t}, where

zt,i:=(gt,It−B)𝟏{It=i}pt,i.z_{t,i}:=\frac{(g_{t,I_{t}}-B)\mathbf{1}\{I_{t}=i\}}{p_{t,i}}.

Then 𝔼t​[𝒛t]=𝒈t−B​𝟏\mathbb{E}_{t}[\bm{z}_{t}]=\bm{g}_{t}-B\boldsymbol{1}. Here 𝔼t\mathbb{E}_{t} conditions on the history and the current reward vector, determined before sampling. The common shift leaves linear comparisons unchanged because ⟨𝟏,𝒖−𝒑t⟩=0\langle\boldsymbol{1},\bm{u}-\bm{p}_{t}\rangle=0.

The following second-moment form of the exponential-weights guarantee also accommodates the set-reward estimator used in our reduction. It follows from the standard Hedge/Exp3 analysis in Hazan [2016](Sections 1.3.3 and 6.2.1), retaining DKL(𝒖∥𝒑1)D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\bm{u}\|\bm{p}_{1}) in the bound and using ex≤1+x+x2/2e^{x}\leq 1+x+x^{2}/2 for x≤0x\leq 0. Thus, no uniform bound on the magnitude of the nonpositive estimates is required.

Theorem 8 (Bandit regret).

Suppose the update uses finite feedback 𝐳t≤0\bm{z}_{t}\leq 0 with

𝔼t​[𝒛t]=𝒈t−ct​𝟏,𝔼t​[∑ipt,i​zt,i2]≤V,\mathbb{E}_{t}[\bm{z}_{t}]=\bm{g}_{t}-c_{t}\boldsymbol{1},\qquad\mathbb{E}_{t}\!\left[\sum_{i}p_{t,i}z_{t,i}^{2}\right]\leq V,

where ctc_{t} is determined before the current sample and V>0V>0. For every fixed distribution 𝐮∈Δn\bm{u}\in\Delta_{n} and every η>0\eta>0,

𝔼⁡[∑t=1T⟨𝒈t,𝒖−𝒑t⟩]≤DKL(𝒖∥𝒑1)η+η​T​V2.\mathbb{E}\!\left[\sum_{t=1}^{T}\langle\bm{g}_{t},\bm{u}-\bm{p}_{t}\rangle\right]\leq\frac{D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\bm{u}\|\bm{p}_{1})}{\eta}+\frac{\eta TV}{2}. (14)

For any collection of fixed distributions satisfying DKL(𝐮∥𝐩1)≤DD_{\mathrm{KL}}(\bm{u}\|\bm{p}_{1})\leq D, where D>0D>0, choosing η=2​D/(T​V)\eta=\sqrt{2D/(TV)} gives expected regret at most 2​D​T​V\sqrt{2DTV} against each distribution in the collection.

For the single-arm estimator above, 𝔼t​[∑ipt,i​zt,i2]=∑i(gt,i−B)2≤n​B2\mathbb{E}_{t}[\sum_{i}p_{t,i}z_{t,i}^{2}]=\sum_{i}(g_{t,i}-B)^{2}\leq nB^{2}. Taking D=log⁡nD=\log n therefore bounds regret against the best fixed action:

max⁡∑t=1Ti∈[n]⁡gt,i−𝔼⁡[∑t=1Tgt,It]≤B​2​n​T​log⁡n\max_{i\in[n]}\sum_{t=1}^{T}g_{t,i}-\mathbb{E}\!\left[\sum_{t=1}^{T}g_{t,I_{t}}\right]\leq B\sqrt{2nT\log n}

for an oblivious reward sequence.

In our bandit reduction, the estimator satisfies the theorem with 𝒈t=∇Gt​(𝒑t)\bm{g}_{t}=\nabla G_{t}(\bm{p}_{t}), ct=∑mbmc_{t}=\sum_{m}b_{m}, and V=VqV=V_{q}, as established in the main text. For the uniform distribution 𝒑S\bm{p}^{S} on a fixed kk-element set SS, DKL(𝒑S∥𝒑1)=log(n/k)D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\bm{p}^{S}\|\bm{p}_{1})=\log(n/k), which yields the bound log⁡(n/k)/η+η​T​Vq/2\log(n/k)/\eta+\eta TV_{q}/2 used there to control (1−1/e)(1-1/e)-regret against the best fixed set.

Appendix E Experiments

Our code and data are available on GitHub.

E.1 Datasets and Problem Instances

We evaluate the algorithms on three monotone submodular maximization problems: a weighted influence-maximization instance on Zachary’s Karate Club graph [Zachary, 1977], Influence; a synthetic team-formation instance, TeamFormation; and a synthetic weighted-coverage instance, Coverage.

At every round tt, the learner selects a set St⊆[n]S_{t}\subseteq[n] satisfying |St|≤k|S_{t}|\leq k and observes only the scalar reward ft​(St)f_{t}(S_{t}). The learner does not observe ftf_{t}, its marginal gains, or the rewards of sets that were not selected. All objectives are monotone and submodular. Rewards are normalized to lie in [0,1][0,1] using a common valid upper bound for each problem instance.

For TeamFormation and Coverage, we generate ten base task types and sample the task type at each round independently and uniformly. For Influence, we independently sample a new live-edge graph at every round. Table 2 summarizes the instance parameters.

Influence. The Influence instance is defined on Zachary’s Karate Club graph, which contains n=34n=34 vertices and 7878 undirected edges. At each round, every edge is independently retained with probability p=0.05p=0.05, producing a live-edge realization of the graph.

The reward of a seed set SS is the total weight of the vertices reachable from at least one seed in SS. Equivalently, it is the total weight of the connected components intersected by SS. This is a weighted coverage function and is therefore monotone and submodular [Kempe et al., 2003].

Vertices 00 and 3333 receive weight 0.50.5, while every other vertex receives weight 0.010.01. We use the cardinality constraint k=2k=2 and normalize rewards by the total vertex weight, which equals 1.321.32.

Team Formation. The TeamFormation instance models roster selection over a pool of n=100n=100 candidates. The learner selects a team of at most k=3k=3 candidates. For task type τ\tau, the reward is the monotone submodular quadratic function

fτ​(𝒚)=𝒘τ⊺​𝒚+12​𝒚⊺​𝑯τ​𝒚,\displaystyle f_{\tau}(\bm{y})=\bm{w}_{\tau}^{\intercal}\bm{y}+\frac{1}{2}\bm{y}^{\intercal}\bm{H}_{\tau}\bm{y},

where 𝒚∈{0,1}n\bm{y}\in\{0,1\}^{n} indicates the selected team, 𝒘τ∈ℝ≥0n\bm{w}_{\tau}\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}^{n} contains the individual candidate values, and 𝑯τ\bm{H}_{\tau} models redundancy between candidates with similar skills.

Each candidate ii is assigned a fixed embedding 𝒔i∈ℝ8\bm{s}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{8}, sampled from 𝒩⁡(0,I8)\mathcal{N}(0,I_{8}). We sample a common unit requirement vector 𝒓¯\bar{\bm{r}} and define the requirement vector of task type τ\tau as

𝒓τ=𝒓¯+0.05​𝝃τ‖𝒓¯+0.05​𝝃τ‖2,\displaystyle\bm{r}_{\tau}=\frac{\bar{\bm{r}}+0.05\,\boldsymbol{\xi}_{\tau}}{\|\bar{\bm{r}}+0.05\,\boldsymbol{\xi}_{\tau}\|_{2}},

where 𝝃τ\boldsymbol{\xi}_{\tau} is an independently sampled unit vector. The ten task types therefore have related, but nonidentical, skill requirements.

The raw score of candidate ii on task τ\tau uses its normalized embedding:

40​⟨𝒔i‖𝒔i‖2,𝒓τ⟩+ϵτ,i,ϵτ,i∼𝒩⁡(0,1).\displaystyle 40\left\langle\frac{\bm{s}_{i}}{\|\bm{s}_{i}\|_{2}},\bm{r}_{\tau}\right\rangle+\epsilon_{\tau,i},\qquad\epsilon_{\tau,i}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1).

The scores are shifted and rescaled to [0,100][0,100]. We designate 75%75\% of the candidates as permanently low-value candidates. Among the remaining candidates, only the ten highest-scoring candidates for each task retain their similarity-based scores. Every other candidate receives a small value sampled from [0.05,0.5][0.05,0.5].

To model overlap between candidates, we construct a 1515-nearest-neighbor graph using cosine similarity between their embeddings. For every edge (i,j)(i,j), we set

(𝑯τ)i​j=(𝑯τ)j​i=−λτ​max⁡{0,cos⁡(𝒔i,𝒔j)}​min⁡{wτ,i,wτ,j}k−1,\displaystyle(\bm{H}_{\tau})_{ij}=(\bm{H}_{\tau})_{ji}=-\lambda_{\tau}\max\{0,\cos(\bm{s}_{i},\bm{s}_{j})\}\frac{\min\{w_{\tau,i},w_{\tau,j}\}}{k-1},

where λτ\lambda_{\tau} is sampled uniformly from [0.05,0.15][0.05,0.15]. All remaining entries are zero. The nonpositive pairwise terms imply submodularity. For any feasible addition to a set of fewer than kk candidates, the total reduction in the marginal value of candidate ii is at most λτ​wτ,i<wτ,i\lambda_{\tau}w_{\tau,i}<w_{\tau,i}, so the objective is monotone on the feasible region. For the fixed evaluation and tuning instances, we also verified wτ,i+∑j≠i(𝑯τ)i​j>0w_{\tau,i}+\sum_{j\neq i}(\bm{H}_{\tau})_{ij}>0 for every task and candidate; hence their objectives are monotone on all subsets.

We sample a length-T=105T=10^{5} stream independently and uniformly from the ten task types. Rewards are normalized by the largest, across task types, sum of the kk largest individual candidate values. This is a valid upper bound because the quadratic term is nonpositive.

Coverage. The Coverage instance is a weighted coverage problem with n=100n=100 selectable elements, cardinality constraint k=3k=3, and a universe of 250250 features. The universe consists of ten topics with 2020 features each and 5050 low-value background features. Each element ii covers a fixed subset CiC_{i} of the feature universe. For task type τ\tau, the reward is

fτ​(S)=∑u∈⋃i∈SCiaτ,u,\displaystyle f_{\tau}(S)=\sum_{u\in\bigcup_{i\in S}C_{i}}a_{\tau,u},

where aτ,u≥0a_{\tau,u}\geq 0 is the task-dependent weight of feature uu. This is a monotone submodular weighted coverage function.

We generate ten related task types. Three topics are shared across all tasks, with feature weights sampled from [0.8,1.2][0.8,1.2]. Each task also emphasizes one of the remaining seven topics, whose feature weights are sampled from [0.15,0.30][0.15,0.30]. Features in all other topics receive weights in [0.01,0.03][0.01,0.03], while background features receive weights in [0.001,0.005][0.001,0.005].

We designate 75%75\% of the elements as low-value elements, each covering only two background features. Of the remaining elements, ten are topic specialists. Each specialist covers 1616 features from one topic and two background features. Ten shared generalists each cover eight features from every shared topic and two background features. The final five generalists cover three features from each of three randomly selected topics and two background features.

We sample a length-T=105T=10^{5} stream independently and uniformly from the ten task types. Rewards are normalized by the maximum total feature weight of any task type. This is a valid upper bound because no selected set can cover more than the complete feature universe.

E.2 Algorithms

Sub-EW. We evaluate our bandit algorithm, denoted by Sub-EW. At each round, Sub-EW samples a draw count from the distribution prescribed by Algorithm 2, draws that many elements independently with replacement from its current exponential-weights distribution, and plays their union. It updates its distribution using only the normalized reward of the selected set and the importance-weighted estimator developed in the paper.

Baselines. We compare Sub-EW with six baselines:

  • •

    Random selects a uniformly random subset of exactly kk distinct elements at every round.

  • •

    MSE3 implements Algorithm 1 of Pasteris et al. [2024]. Like Sub-EW, it maintains one item distribution and samples with replacement, but always makes kk draws. It estimates the gradient of the fixed-draw expected reward, and its guarantee relies on pseudo-concavity.

  • •

    OpaqueGreedy implements the opaque-feedback greedy algorithm of Streeter and Golovin [2008]. It maintains one weighted-majority learner per greedy stage and uses prefix-plus-element exploration.

  • •

    Bandit-IG implements Algorithms 3–4 and Example 1 of Niazadeh et al. [2023]. Each greedy stage has a Hedge learner that instantiates the required Blackwell-approachability subroutine. After its rrth feedback update, that learner uses weights wr+1,i∝exp(−ηr∑s=1rℓ^s,i)w_{r+1,i}\propto\exp(-\eta_{r}\sum_{s=1}^{r}\widehat{\ell}_{s,i}).

  • •

    BanditMLSM specializes Algorithms 2 and 4 of Wan et al. [2023] to one partition group of capacity kk. Its product of kk simplexes includes a dummy option in each factor, so a sampled set contains at most kk elements. One exploration round per block provides a scalar-feedback gradient estimate for its log-barrier follow-the-regularized-leader update.

  • •

    Poisson-BE specializes Algorithm 2 of Wan and Zhang [2026] to the uniform rank-kk matroid. It uses a Poisson base walk and balanced exchanges, estimates an insertion loss from one feasible-set reward, and applies an entropy update followed by projection onto a shrunken base polytope.

Every algorithm observes only the normalized reward of its selected set.

Hyperparameters. For Sub-EW, MSE3, OpaqueGreedy, and Bandit-IG, we multiply the prescribed learning rate by cη∈{0.25,1,4,16,64}c_{\eta}\in\{0.25,1,4,16,64\}. For each dataset and algorithm, we select the candidate with the highest mean normalized reward over three independent repetitions on a separately generated tuning instance. The tuning horizon is min⁡{T,104}\min\{T,10^{4}\}. The multiplier cη=1c_{\eta}=1 is evaluated first and wins ties.

OpaqueGreedy uses exploration probability γ=min⁡{1,k​(n​log⁡n/T)1/3}\gamma=\min\{1,k(n\log n/T)^{1/3}\}, and Bandit-IG uses q=min⁡{1,(n2​log⁡n/T)1/3}q=\min\{1,(n^{2}\log n/T)^{1/3}\}. For Bandit-IG, TT in this formula and in its Hedge schedule is the evaluation horizon, even when candidates are scored on shorter tuning streams. The selected multipliers are reported in Table 3.

BanditMLSM and Poisson-BE use separate practical tuning grids. For BanditMLSM, we tune the block length L∈{8,32,128,512}L\in\{8,32,128,512\} and the learning rate η=cηd−4T−2/3\eta=c_{\eta}d^{-4}T^{-2/3}, where d=n​kd=nk. The unscaled rate comes from Wan et al.’s Algorithm 1 and serves only as a practical tuning reference for our product-simplex implementation. The multiplier grid is {104,105,106,107}\{10^{4},10^{5},10^{6},10^{7}\} for Influence and {106,107,108}\{10^{6},10^{7},10^{8}\} for TeamFormation and Coverage. For Poisson-BE, we tune exploration probability γ∈{0.05,0.2,0.5}\gamma\in\{0.05,0.2,0.5\} and a multiplier cη∈{0.25,1,4,16,64,256}c_{\eta}\in\{0.25,1,4,16,64,256\} of k2​γ​log⁡(e​n)/(2​n​(μ2+μ)​T)\sqrt{k^{2}\gamma\log(en)/(2n(\mu^{2}+\mu)T)}, where μ=k​log⁡T\mu=k\log T. Its starting time ε=1/T\varepsilon=1/T, shrinkage δ=min⁡{1/2,1/(μ​T)}\delta=\min\{1/2,1/(\mu T)\}, and Poisson event cap ⌈2​e​(μ+log⁡T)⌉\lceil 2e(\mu+\log T)\rceil follow the published formulas. Both methods use the evaluation horizon to compute their parameter values and three independent shorter tuning streams for candidate selection.

For the product-simplex wrapper, the proof of Lemma 5.1 in Wan et al. uses η=d−7/3T−1/3\eta=d^{-7/3}T^{-1/3} and L=d−5/3T1/3L=d^{-5/3}T^{1/3}. The latter is below one round at our dimensions. Poisson-BE’s learning-regime condition n⁡(μ2+μ)​log⁡(e​n)<Tn(\mu^{2}+\mu)\log(en)<T also does not hold. The tuned configurations retain the published sampling and update rules; they are practical instantiations rather than finite-horizon applications of those theorems. Table 4 reports their selected parameters.

E.3 Evaluation Protocol

Average approximate regret. For each evaluation stream and every round tt, let

OPTt=maxS:|S|≤k∑s=1tfs(S).\displaystyle\mathrm{OPT}_{t}=\max_{S:\,|S|\leq k}\sum_{s=1}^{t}f_{s}(S).

The maximization selects one fixed set for the entire prefix of length tt; the maximizing set may differ between prefixes. We report

AAR⁡(t)=1t​[(1−1/e)​OPTt−∑s=1tfs​(Ss)].\displaystyle\mathrm{AAR}(t)=\frac{1}{t}\left[(1-1/e)\mathrm{OPT}_{t}-\sum_{s=1}^{t}f_{s}(S_{s})\right].

Lower values are better. A negative value means that the algorithm’s cumulative reward exceeds (1−1/e)​OPTt(1-1/e)\mathrm{OPT}_{t}.

We compute OPTt\mathrm{OPT}_{t} at every timestep by exhaustive enumeration with cumulative candidate scores. Monotonicity permits enumeration of sets of size exactly kk: there are (342)=561\binom{34}{2}=561 candidates for Influence and (1003)=161,700\binom{100}{3}=161{,}700 for each of TeamFormation and Coverage. For the latter two datasets, we precompute each candidate’s reward for the ten task types. A common maximizer of all task types is used to obtain the prefix trajectory only after verifying that property for the loaded instance; otherwise, we update all candidate scores at each prefix. The metric is computed at every timestep, even when a figure displays a subsampled curve.

Repetitions. We perform ten independent evaluation repetitions for every dataset. Within a repetition, all algorithms are evaluated on the same task stream, while each algorithm uses its own random seed. Across repetitions, both the task stream and the algorithmic random seeds change. The underlying graph, candidate embeddings, task types, and coverage sets remain fixed.

The reported curve is the pointwise mean of AAR⁡(t)\mathrm{AAR}(t) over the ten evaluation repetitions. The shaded region extends one sample standard deviation above and below the mean.

Reproducibility. The implementation uses Python 3.10.10, NumPy 2.2.6, SciPy 1.15.3, NetworkX 3.4.2, and Matplotlib 3.10.9. The repository contains the source code, fixed problem instances, configuration files, tests, and plotting scripts.

Setup. All experiments were run on an Apple M2 MacBook with 16 GB of RAM.
